finding: Gin 1990 (read in full): 10 women at caesarean (65.3 kg) against 6 nonpregnant women at laparoscopic sterilisation (52.8 kg), 2 mg/kg, whole blood to 480 min, non-compartmental: CL 2.55 (0.49) vs 1.57 (0.56) L/min (P < 0.01), 39.32 vs 29.40 mL/kg/min (P < 0.05); Vss 2.66 vs 3.36 L/kg and half-life 81 vs 99 min, not significant. The authors raised blood loss and delivery as a possible cause. Gin 1991 (read in full): 8 women at caesarean against 8 women 2-3 days postpartum given 2 mg/kg for sterilisation, whole blood sampled to 600 min, non-compartmental: CL 31.5 (24.4-53.3) vs 33.8 (21.5-47.2) mL/min/kg, Vss 5.10 vs 5.17 L/kg (medians). The comparator is NOT nonpregnant: the authors chose women 2-3 days postpartum because they keep most of the physiology of pregnancy without the blood loss and loss of the fetus and placenta, and conclude that the two groups are alike and that the rise in clearance at caesarean is not from the operation, so postpartum pharmacokinetics are 'closer to those in patients undergoing Caesarean section than those in non-pregnant patients'. Clearance at caesarean exceeded their nonpregnant group of 1990 (P < 0.05), but sampling times differed between the studies, and per kilogram the 1991 caesarean median is only 7% above the 1990 nonpregnant mean (31.5 vs 29.4), against 34% in the 1990 comparison itself; the caesarean women weighed 72.5 kg against 62.0 postpartum. Against the library's Eleveld model, which reproduces Gin 1990's nonpregnant group (1.55 vs 1.57 L/min at 52.8 kg, 33.3 y), clearance was 1.39 times the model at caesarean in 1990, 1.15 times in 1991 (longer sampling) and 1.19 times 2-3 days postpartum. Kanto 1990 (8 parturients, no control): CL 2189.6 mL/min, t1/2 24.1 min. Pharmacodynamically, the C50 for loss of consciousness is unchanged in the first trimester (Higuchi 2001: 2.0 vs 2.1 ug/mL) or slightly lower (Mongardon 2009: predicted Ce at LOC 4.59 vs 5.01 ug/mL, -8%).
applied: Elimination clearance × 1.28: each caesarean group's clearance (Gin 1990, 1991) over this model's for a nonpregnant woman of the same age and weight, geometric mean weighted by group size; volumes unchanged; the same factor on the Schnider companion.
trimester: third (term caesarean); PD data first trimester
comparator: non-pregnant women (Gin 1990); postpartum women, different individuals (Gin 1991)
design: cross-sectional NCA against the library model
source: Gin T, Gregory MA, Chan K, Buckley T, Oh TE. Pharmacokinetics of propofol in women undergoing elective caesarean section. Br J Anaesth 1990;64:148-153 PMID 2138487; Gin T, Yau G, Jong W, Tan P, Leung RK, Chan K. Disposition of propofol at caesarean section and in the postpartum period. Br J Anaesth 1991;67:49-53 PMID 1859759; Kanto J, Rosenberg P. Propofol in cesarean section. A pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic study. Methods Find Exp Clin Pharmacol 1990;12:707-711 PMID 2100757; Higuchi H, Adachi Y, Arimura S, Kanno M, Satoh T. Early pregnancy does not reduce the C50 of propofol for loss of consciousness. Anesth Analg 2001;93:1565-1569 PMID 11726445; Mongardon N, Servin F, Perrin M, et al. Predicted propofol effect-site concentration for induction and emergence of anesthesia during early pregnancy. Anesth Analg 2009;109:90-95 PMID 19439683; Dailland P, Cockshott ID, Lirzin JD, et al. Intravenous propofol during cesarean section: placental transfer, concentrations in breast milk, and neonatal effects. Anesthesiology 1989;71:827-834 PMID 2589672; Sanchez-Alcaraz A, Quintana MB, Laguarda M. Placental transfer and neonatal effects of propofol in caesarean section. J Clin Pharm Ther 1998;23:19-23 PMID 9756107
notes: Whole-blood HPLC assays in Gin/Dailland; the Eleveld model is arterial/venous plasma. Free fraction: maternal unbound propofol 1.75 +/- 0.36% (range 1.28-2.29%; Gin 1991), not compared to non-pregnant. Gin 1991 used enflurane and nitrous oxide after induction and morphine after delivery at caesarean, none postpartum. Placental transfer UV/MV 0.62-0.86 (Gin 1991), 0.70-0.76 (Dailland 1989). Propofol clearance is near hepatic blood flow and largely extrahepatic, so the CYP-induction mechanism does not translate.

finding: The library already applies CL x2 from Ansari 2016 (Table 3, citing Kan 1998). Kan 1998 (n=19 parturients, cesarean, 0.1 mcg/kg/min infusion, term) reported mean total remifentanil clearance 93 mL/min/kg, roughly 2-2.3x the ~40 mL/min/kg of non-pregnant adults, which is the basis for 'clearance more than doubles'. A newer mid-trimester study (Smith 2017, n=8, fetal surgery, 22 weeks) instead found clearance 170.7 L/h, LOWER than the non-pregnant 250-300 L/h (a 1.8-fold decrease) with volume of distribution ~3.3x higher and roughly doubled alpha-1-acid glycoprotein; the authors attribute the lower clearance to high AAG from surgical stress and it is mid-trimester. Remifentanil is cleared by nonspecific esterases, not CYP or kidney.
applied: Elimination clearance × 2, on the Eleveld and Kim models and on the Minto companion model.
source: Kan RE, Hughes SC, Rosen MA, et al. Anesthesiology 1998;88:1467-1474 PMID 9637638; Smith JA, Donepudi RV, Argoti PS, et al. Front Pharmacol 2017;8:11 PMID 28174536
notes: No change to the existing implementation is indicated. Clearance by esterases means the GFR rise is irrelevant; the two primary datasets disagree in direction, so x2 (term, Kan) is retained rather than refined. Total plasma concentration is plotted; higher AAG binding in pregnancy would lower free fraction but the library plots total.

finding: No human IV population PK study in pregnancy yields a parent-fentanyl clearance ratio. Fentanyl is eliminated almost entirely by CYP3A4 N-dealkylation to norfentanyl. CYP3A activity rises 35-38% across all trimesters (Tracy 2005, paired dextromethorphan phenotyping, n=25) and retrospective TDM in pregnant opioid users shows a higher norfentanyl/fentanyl metabolic ratio (faster conversion) with advancing gestation (Wanar 2022/2023). Human obstetric fentanyl data are epidural/apparent only (Moises 2005: CL/F 6.875 mL/min/kg).
source: Tracy TS, Venkataramanan R, Glover DD, Caritis SN. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2005;192:633-639 PMID 15696014; Wanar A, Saia K, Field TA. Matern Child Health J 2023;27:1944-1948 PMID 37269392; Moises ECD, de Barros Duarte L, et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2005;61:517-522 PMID 16021436
notes: The library's current row is 'unknown'; this review upgrades it to a documented direction (clearance up via CYP3A4 induction) but no drug-specific magnitude. Shum 2021 mf-PBPK (PMID 34407992) models maternal-fetal fentanyl but does not report a maternal clearance ratio; full text would not add a usable factor. Total plasma plotted.

finding: Gepts 1986 gave 30 mcg/kg IV alfentanil to pregnant women at cesarean (n=5) and compared with non-pregnant surgical women (n=5): terminal half-life 103 min, Vdss 541 mL/kg, total plasma clearance 6.48 mL/kg/min, none differing significantly from non-pregnant. This is the basis for Ansari 2016's 'no change in volume of distribution or clearance', which the library already encodes as 'unchanged'.
source: Gepts E, Heytens L, Camu F. Anesth Analg 1986;65:1155-1160 PMID 2876662
notes: Matches the existing library finding. Total plasma plotted; AAG binding caveat (85-90% bound, higher in maternal plasma) does not change the library's total-concentration output.

finding: No intravenous pregnancy PK with a parent-sufentanil clearance ratio was found. The only pregnancy population PK is epidural and apparent (Nie 2025, n=41 labouring women, co-infused with ropivacaine): CL/F 176 L/h, V1/F 519 L for a two-compartment maternal model, which cannot be compared with absolute non-pregnant disposition (the library uses Gepts 1995, IV). Sufentanil is a CYP3A4 substrate, so the CYP3A rise (~35%, Tracy 2005) suggests higher clearance in direction only.
comparator: none (no non-pregnant arm; epidural apparent only)
source: Nie Y, Sun X, Cao R, et al. Drug Des Devel Ther 2025;19:971-980 PMID 39963603
notes: Total plasma plotted; sufentanil is ~93% protein bound. The epidural route and ropivacaine co-administration make the Nie 2025 CL/F unusable for the library's IV model.

finding: The library already applies elimination CL x1.7 (Ansari 2016, citing Gerdin 1990). Gerdin 1990 studied 13 nulliparous parturients (IV or IM morphine) vs 6 non-pregnant women: plasma clearance 3.4 vs 2.0 L/min (ratio 1.7), elimination half-life 43 vs 84 min, apparent volume of distribution unchanged, and faster/larger M3G formation. Morphine is cleared by UGT2B7 glucuronidation, which is induced in pregnancy.
applied: Elimination clearance × 1.7; volumes and distribution clearances unchanged.
source: Gerdin E, Salmonson T, Lindberg B, Rane A. J Perinat Med 1990;18:479-487 PMID 2097341
notes: No change indicated. Morphine-6-glucuronide (active, formed faster in pregnancy) is not modelled in the library, so the understatement of oral effect noted in the model header persists. Total plasma plotted.

finding: Ansari 2016 classes pethidine as unchanged (increased CYP3A4 inactivation balanced by decreased clearance; no half-life change), which the library encodes. Direct data are mixed: Tomson 1982 (n=16, IM in labour) found half-life 3.4 h 'not different from healthy controls'; Kuhnert 1980 found no significant difference in any kinetic constant between peripartum and non-pregnant women; but Morgan 1978 (n=7, IV in labour) found total clearance LOWER in pregnancy (843 vs 1465 mL/min) with smaller distribution volumes. Normeperidine (active, neurotoxic) accumulates with repeated dosing (Kuhnert 1985, half-life ~20 h) but is not modelled.
source: Tomson G, Garle RI, Thalme B, et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 1982;13:653-659 PMID 7082532; Kuhnert BR, Kuhnert PM, Prochaska AL, Sokol RJ. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1980;27:486-491 PMID 7357807; Morgan D, Moore G, Thomas J, Triggs E. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1978;23:288-295 PMID 627134
notes: Matches library. Total plasma plotted; normeperidine not modelled, so neurotoxic-metabolite accumulation with repeated labour dosing is not represented regardless of the flag.

finding: Puhto 2020 (pilot, n=7, single epidural dose in labour) found median terminal half-life 162 min (range 87-260), similar to the ~184 min reported in non-pregnant adults after IV hydromorphone, and distribution/elimination 'fairly similar' to non-pregnant IV (the library's Drover 2002 model). Hydromorphone is cleared by UGT2B7; the authors state UGT2B7 activity is unaltered in pregnancy (zidovudine, morphine data), implying little clearance change. The library row is currently 'unknown'.
source: Puhto T, Kokki M, Hakomaki H, et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2020;76:969-977 PMID 32363420
notes: This upgrades the library's 'unknown' to 'unchanged (low confidence)'. Epidural route, n=7, short terminal sampling; a definitive IV pregnancy PK does not exist. Total plasma plotted.

finding: The library applies CL x24/14 = 1.71 to both enantiomers (Ansari 2016, half-life 8-20 h in pregnancy vs 24 h non-pregnant). Newer primary data confirm and slightly strengthen this. Bogen 2012 (n=25, longitudinal) measured third-trimester enantiomer half-lives R 14.7-24.9 h and S 8.02-18.9 h, about half of non-pregnant, with R/S/rac clearances significantly larger in pregnancy than postpartum; rac half-life in pregnancy 11-21 h vs 22-54 h non-pregnant. Pond 1985 and Wolff 2005 (weight-adjusted CL 0.17 to 0.21 L/h/kg across pregnancy) and McCarthy 2018 (methadone/metabolite ratio falling across trimesters) agree. Mechanism: CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 induction (CYP2B6 induced by estradiol ~1.5-3x, Dickmann 2012).
applied: Clearance of both enantiomers × 24/14 = 1.71, the 24-hour half-life over the midpoint of 8 to 20 hours; volumes unchanged.
source: Bogen DL, Perel JM, Helsel JC, et al. Psychopharmacology 2012;225:441-451 PMID 22926004; Pond SM, Kreek MJ, Tong TG, et al. J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1985;233:1-6 PMID 3981450; McCarthy JJ, Vasti EJ, Leamon MH, et al. J Addict Med 2018;12:241-246 PMID 29521669; Wolff K, Boys A, Rostami-Hodjegan A, et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2005;61:763-768 PMID 16261362; Dickmann LJ, Isoherranen N. Drug Metab Dispos 2013;41:270-274 PMID 22815312
notes: No change to the existing x1.71 is needed; newer Bogen/McCarthy data corroborate it. The model header already notes the CYP2B6-phenotype x pregnancy interaction is unquantified and left multiplicative; that remains correct. Total plasma (racemic base) plotted.

finding: No human study of ketamine (racemic or S-) pharmacokinetics in pregnant versus non-pregnant women was found. Retrieved literature is sheep placental transfer (Musk 2011: no difference in maternal plasma concentration between pregnant and non-pregnant ewes over 10 min), maternal/fetal concentrations at caesarean (Adams 2003: esketamine maternal 493 vs fetal 251 ng/mL), and breast-milk studies.
source: Musk GC, Netto JD, Maker GL, Trengove RD. Transplacental transfer of medetomidine and ketamine in pregnant ewes. Lab Anim 2011;46:46-50 PMID 22008849; Adams HA, Meyer P, Stoppa A, et al. [Anaesthesia for caesarean section...] Anaesthesist 2003;52:23-32 PMID 12577162
notes: Ketamine is CYP3A4/2B6 metabolised and has a high hepatic extraction; a pregnancy rise in CYP3A4/2B6 activity would be expected to matter little for IV clearance (flow-limited). Ansari 2016 row: unknown, unchanged in the pregnant ewe.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic study of IV dexmedetomidine in pregnancy with a non-pregnant or postpartum comparator was found. Retrieved data are placental transfer at caesarean (Wang 2017: UV/maternal ratio 0.68 after 0.5 ug/kg then 0.5 ug/kg/h under epidural) and an ewe assay paper.
source: Wang C, Liu S, Han C, Yu M, Hu Y, Liu C. Effect and placental transfer of dexmedetomidine during caesarean section under epidural anaesthesia. J Int Med Res 2017;45:964-972 PMID 28449631
notes: Dexmedetomidine is highly protein bound (~94%) and glucuronidated/CYP2A6-metabolised; both pathways may rise in pregnancy (UGT, CYP2A6 induced), so clearance would plausibly rise, but no magnitude exists.

finding: Wilson 1987 (read in full; the one intravenous comparison): 5 mg IV, plasma to 2 h, non-compartmental; clearance 6.5 mL/min/kg in active labour (n = 12), 9.0 awaiting caesarean section 3 h before surgery (n = 10, 73 kg), 13.9 at the start of caesarean section (n = 8), 8.7 and 7.0 in two nonpregnant gynaecological groups (n = 10 each, 60 kg, one given oxytocin). Against this model at each group's age and weight, the awaiting group is 1.28 times the gynaecological groups, labour 0.91. Hebert 2008: 13 women given 2 mg ORAL midazolam at 28-32 weeks and again 6-10 weeks postpartum (paired NCA): total CL/F 4.2 vs 2.0 L/min (ratio 2.1) and unbound CL/F 593 +/- 237 vs 345 +/- 103 (ratio 1.72), with the terminal half-life unchanged (2.4 vs 2.5 h) and Cmax 28% lower (full text now read). Quinney 2012 (same data, full text in PMC) reports the observed total oral AUC 9.5 ng.h/mL in pregnancy vs 17.4 postpartum (total CL/F ratio 17.4/9.5 = 1.83) and, fitting a semi-mechanistic model, attributes it to hepatic CYP3A intrinsic clearance x1.6 with an unchanged gut-wall extraction, plus a 20% higher unbound fraction. IV data are conflicting and older: Wilson 1987 found the LOWEST clearance and smallest volume in women in active labour (5 mg IV, radio-sampled 2 h; no numbers in abstract); Kanto 1984 (6 women immediately after caesarean delivery, radioreceptor assay) found CL 13.18 mL/min/kg, 1.72x this library's 7.64 mL/min/kg at 70 kg.
applied: Elimination clearance × 1.28: Wilson 1987's women awaiting caesarean section over its gynaecological women, each set against this model at its own age and weight; Hebert 2008's paired oral data, carried to an intravenous dose through Quinney's mechanism, give 1.45. Volumes unchanged; active labour (×0.91) is not represented.
comparator: nonpregnant gynaecological women (Wilson); postpartum, same women (Hebert)
design: IV NCA against nonpregnant women and the library model (Wilson); paired oral NCA (Hebert)
source: Hebert MF, Easterling TR, Kirby B, et al. Effects of pregnancy on CYP3A and P-glycoprotein activities as measured by disposition of midazolam and digoxin: a University of Washington specialized center of research study. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2008;84:248-253 PMID 18288078; Quinney SK, Mohamed AN, Hebert MF, et al. A semi-mechanistic metabolism model of CYP3A substrates in pregnancy: predicting changes in midazolam and nifedipine pharmacokinetics. CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2012;1:e2 PMID 23835882; Wilson CM, Dundee JW, Moore J, Howard PJ, Collier PS. A comparison of the early pharmacokinetics of midazolam in pregnant and nonpregnant women. Anaesthesia 1987;42:1057-1062 PMID 3688386; Kanto J, Aaltonen L, Erkkola R, Aarimaa L. Pharmacokinetics and sedative effect of midazolam in connection with caesarean section performed under epidural analgesia. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1984;28:116-118 PMID 6711257; Andrew MA, Hebert MF, Vicini P. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic model of midazolam disposition during pregnancy. Conf Proc IEEE Eng Med Biol Soc 2008:5454-5457 PMID 19163951
notes: Ansari 2016 lists midazolam as direction only (lower peak, unchanged half-life); Wilson's intravenous groups and Hebert's paired oral data supersede that. Wilson sampled only 2 h, so absolute clearances are high; the ratio between groups sampled alike is what is used. Hebert's ratio is unbound and oral; total plasma (which the library plots) rises by about 1.83 orally. The IV factor 1.45 depends on the assumed hepatic blood flow (QH 1.5 L/min; with QH 2.0 L/min the same arithmetic gives 1.55) and on Quinney's assumption that hepatic blood flow is unchanged. Labour itself may reduce clearance (Wilson 1987). Unbound fraction rises ~20% (albumin 38.8 vs 47.7 g/L, quoted in Quinney), so free midazolam rises relative to total.

finding: No pregnant-vs-non-pregnant etomidate pharmacokinetics found. Esener 1992 reports maternal plasma concentrations after induction for caesarean section (1242 ng/mL at 5 min, 434 at 15, 64.2 at 30, 7.0 at 60 min; n = 40 with thiopentone) without a non-pregnant control; Liu 2025 gives placental transfer 0.75.
source: Esener Z, Sarihasan B, Guven H, Ustun E. Thiopentone and etomidate concentrations in maternal and umbilical plasma, and in colostrum. Br J Anaesth 1992;69:586-588 PMID 1467101; Liu H, Cai M, Peng Y, Miao JK, Yu J. A pilot study on LC-MS/MS quantification of remifentanil, etomidate, and rocuronium in maternal and fetal serum microsamples. Sci Rep 2025;15:25876 PMID 40670482
notes: Esener's curve could be compared against the Arden model for a 0.3 mg/kg-type dose if the dose and sampling details (full text) were obtained, but it is not a controlled comparison. Ansari 2016 row: unknown.

finding: No human study compares intravenous lidocaine disposition in pregnant and non-pregnant women. The only parturient data are after epidural or perineal injection, where absorption and disposition are confounded: apparent clearance 6.1 mL/kg/min (epidural with epinephrine, n=10, Downing 1997), 10.1 mL/kg/min (epidural, n=10), 10.6 mL/kg/min (CL/F, epidural, n=10, Moises 2008) and 12.2 mL/kg/min (perineal, n=23, Cavalli 2004), with no non-pregnant arm. The review (Ansari 2016) lists lidocaine as unknown; pregnant/non-pregnant sheep studies exist but are not transferable.
source: Downing JW et al. The pharmacokinetics of epidural lidocaine and bupivacaine during cesarean section. Anesth Analg 1997;84:527-32 PMID 9052295; Cavalli RC et al. Pharmacokinetics and transplacental transfer of lidocaine and its metabolite for perineal analgesic assistance to pregnant women. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2004;60:569-74 PMID 15365654; Moises EC et al. Pharmacokinetics of lidocaine and its metabolite in peridural anesthesia administered to pregnant women with gestational diabetes mellitus. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2008;64:1189-96 PMID 18679666; Sanchez-Alcaraz A et al. [Pharmacokinetics of lidocaine in obstetric patients after its epidural single-dose administration]. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 1997;44:13-5 PMID 9148343
notes: All values are apparent (after extravascular injection) and come from parturients without a non-pregnant control, so they cannot be turned into a ratio. Lidocaine is an intermediate-to-high extraction drug bound to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AAG), which falls in pregnancy, so the unbound fraction is expected to rise; the library plots total concentration. Not worth a Stanford request: no paper with an intravenous pregnant-vs-non-pregnant comparison was found.

finding: After epidural bupivacaine, six term parturients and six non-pregnant women under 65 had a similar time to peak (about 0.4 h) and no significant difference in terminal half-life (Pihlajamaki 1990, read in full: 1.78 vs 1.58 mg/kg). Dose- and weight-normalised Cmax was 0.90 vs 0.64 mg/L and 24-h AUC 5.16 vs 3.31 h.mg/L, neither significant; only the raw Cmax (1.39 vs 0.89) was, from the larger dose. The 24-h AUC is truncated against a 12-15 h apparent half-life (absorption-limited), so no clearance can be derived. What does change is binding: the unbound fraction at term was 8.2% against 5.4% in non-pregnant volunteers (ratio 1.52), with AAG 0.42 against 1.01 g/L (Wulf 1991). Tsen 1999 (n=81) found the free fraction rising with gestation at 5 mcg/mL but not at 1 mcg/mL. No intravenous pregnant-vs-non-pregnant study exists.
source: Pihlajamaki K et al. Extradural administration of bupivacaine: pharmacokinetics and metabolism in pregnant and non-pregnant women. Br J Anaesth 1990;64:556-62 PMID 2354094; Wulf H, Munstedt P, Maier C. Plasma protein binding of bupivacaine in pregnant women at term. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1991;35:129-33 PMID 2024561; Tsen LC et al. Measurements of maternal protein binding of bupivacaine throughout pregnancy. Anesth Analg 1999;89:965-8 PMID 10512273; Denson DD et al. Bupivacaine protein binding in the term parturient: effects of lactic acidosis. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1984;35:702-9 PMID 6713783
notes: Total vs unbound: the library plots total bupivacaine. In a parturient the same total concentration carries about 1.5 times the unbound drug (8.2/5.4), which matters for toxicity but not for the plotted curve. Denson 1984 says the binding change is confined to low total concentrations (<10 mcg/mL). The Ansari row already says 'unchanged'; this review agrees.

finding: No human study compares ropivacaine clearance in pregnant and non-pregnant women. Parturient studies (epidural, Datta 1995 n=20, Irestedt 1997 n=16, McCrae 1997) report only that clearance was 'similar to values reported previously'. In ewes, pregnancy halved total clearance (21.6 vs 45.1 mL/min/kg) and halved the terminal volume with an unchanged half-life, an animal finding that is not transferable. AAG falls in pregnancy and Porter 2001 showed the free fraction of ropivacaine tracks 1/AAG.
source: Irestedt L et al. Ropivacaine 7.5 mg/ml for elective caesarean section. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1997;41:1149-56 PMID 9366935; Datta S et al. Clinical effects and maternal and fetal plasma concentrations of epidural ropivacaine versus bupivacaine for cesarean section. Anesthesiology 1995;82:1346-52 PMID 7793647; Santos AC et al. Pharmacokinetics of ropivacaine in nonpregnant and pregnant ewes. Anesth Analg 1990;70:262-6 PMID 2305977; Porter JM et al. Epidural ropivacaine hydrochloride during labour: protein binding, placental transfer and neonatal outcome. Anaesthesia 2001;56:418-23 PMID 11350325
notes: Sheep data run opposite to the human hepatic-enzyme expectation (CYP1A2, ropivacaine's main pathway, falls in pregnancy; CYP3A4 rises) and should not be used. Unbound fraction likely higher at term (lower AAG); library plots total.

finding: Only single-arm parturient data were found: spinal mepivacaine 60 mg at caesarean (n=11) gave a free maternal concentration of 0.18 mcg/mL at delivery (Bremerich 2003), and a Japanese epidural study (Baba 1987) has no abstract. No pregnant-vs-non-pregnant comparison exists. The review lists mepivacaine as unknown.
source: Bremerich DH et al. Mepivacaine for spinal anesthesia in parturients undergoing elective cesarean delivery. Zentralbl Gynakol 2003;125:518-21 PMID 14755363
notes: Mepivacaine is AAG-bound like bupivacaine, so its unbound fraction is expected to rise at term; the plotted total curve is unaffected by that in any quantifiable way.

finding: Hodge 2026 (popPK, 10 women at term caesarean, median weight 78 kg): rocuronium V 17.9 L and CL 12.6 L/h, 'at the upper end of published ranges from non-pregnant patients' (no control arm). Pharmacodynamics: block lasts longer in pregnancy and postpartum -- Jun 2018 second trimester 45.7 vs 40.6 min to 25% T1 (n = 47/47); Puhringer 1997 postpartum 31.1 vs 24.9 min (n = 12/12); Gin 2002 postpartum 35.3 vs 24.8 min when dosed by total body weight, but the same as controls when dosed by lean body mass (n = 22/22), i.e. explained by relative overdose.
source: Hodge AT, Tognolini AR, Liu X, et al. Plasma levels and postpartum breastmilk concentrations of sugammadex: a pharmacokinetic study in women undergoing general anaesthesia for caesarean delivery. Int J Obstet Anesth 2026;66:104874 PMID 41747364; Jun IJ, Jun J, Kim EM, et al. Comparison of rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade in second trimester pregnant women and non-pregnant women. Int J Obstet Anesth 2018;34:10-14 PMID 29519667; Puhringer FK, Sparr HJ, Mitterschiffthaler G, Agoston S, Benzer A. Extended duration of action of rocuronium in postpartum patients. Anesth Analg 1997;84:352-354 PMID 9024027; Gin T, Chan MT, Chan KL, Yuen PM. Prolonged neuromuscular block after rocuronium in postpartum patients. Anesth Analg 2002;94:686-689 PMID 11867398
notes: Ansari 2016 row: PK unknown, duration possibly prolonged. Caution (outside pregnancy): the library's Plaud 1995 set gives cl1 = 3.92 L x 0.1746 /min = 0.684 L/min (41 L/h) at 70 kg, about three times Hodge's 12.6 L/h and typical adult values (~0.25 L/min); a pregnant/non-pregnant comparison against the library model is therefore not meaningful. Hodge 2026 (read in full) fits rocuronium as three compartments, total V 17.9 L, CL 12.6 L/h, central V1 9.21 L in 10 term women. Placental transfer 0.13 (Liu 2025). Magnesium potentiates block (Gaiser 1996).

finding: Dailey 1984 (read in full; Anesthesiology 60:569-574): 5 women at term caesarean, 0.04 mg/kg, venous serum to 4 h by mass spectrometry: clearance 6.4 +/- 0.4 mL/kg/min, Vss 251 mL/kg, elimination half-life 36 min, no nonpregnant group. This library's model (Vega-Villa 2014) gives 5.7-6.2 mL/kg/min for a nonpregnant woman of 70-80 kg, so the clearance at term is the same within 10%; the smaller volume and shorter half-life reflect 4 h against 12 h of sampling. Dailey 1984: 11 women at caesarean section, 0.04 mg/kg, sampled 4 h: CL 6.4 +/- 0.4 mL/kg/min, t1/2 36 min; no non-pregnant arm. Postpartum (within 4 days) clinical duration is prolonged: Khuenl-Brady 1991 49 vs 32 min (0.1 mg/kg); Hawkins 1989 57.2 vs 35.3 min. Kumagai 1993: in-vitro spontaneous desacetylation unchanged in pregnant plasma. Khuenl-Brady attribute the prolongation to reduced hepatic clearance (hormone competition for uptake), not measured.
source: Dailey PA, Fisher DM, Shnider SM, et al. Pharmacokinetics, placental transfer, and neonatal effects of vecuronium and pancuronium administered during cesarean section. Anesthesiology 1984;60:569-574 PMID 6145374; Khuenl-Brady KS, Koller J, Mair P, Puhringer F, Mitterschiffthaler G. Comparison of vecuronium- and atracurium-induced neuromuscular blockade in postpartum and nonpregnant patients. Anesth Analg 1991;72:110-113 PMID 1670597; Hawkins JL, Adenwala J, Camp C, Joyce TH. The effect of H2-receptor antagonist premedication on the duration of vecuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade in postpartum patients. Anesthesiology 1989;71:175-177 PMID 2569278
notes: Postpartum prolongation may also reflect weight-based dosing (as Gin 2002 showed for rocuronium). Placental transfer UV/MV 0.11 (Dailey).

finding: No pregnancy PK study found. Pan 2001: 22 immediate-postpartum (<48 h) vs 22 non-pregnant women, 0.2 mg/kg: onset faster and clinical duration (25% T1 recovery) SHORTER postpartum, 60 +/- 6 vs 69 +/- 12 min. For atracurium, Khuenl-Brady 1991 found no postpartum change (37 vs 36 min).
source: Pan PH, Moore C. Comparison of cisatracurium-induced neuromuscular blockade between immediate postpartum and nonpregnant patients. J Clin Anesth 2001;13:112-117 PMID 11331170
notes: Faster onset/shorter duration is consistent with a higher cardiac output and, if anything, a larger volume, but no PK was measured.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study giving a maternal clearance or volume ratio was found. Naloxone is cleared mainly by UGT2B7 glucuronidation (plus some reduction); UGT2B7 is reported unaltered in pregnancy (see hydromorphone). The only obstetric data are placental-transfer measurements (Hibbard 1986: rapid transfer after IV, variable after IM) with no pregnant-vs-nonpregnant disposition comparison.
source: Hibbard BM, Rosen M, Davies D. Br J Anaesth 1986;58:45-48 PMID 3942670
notes: UGT2B7 substrate; glucuronidation thought unchanged in pregnancy, consistent with no adjustment. Total plasma plotted.

finding: The human model (Eisenach, unpublished) was fitted in parturients, as R/drugs_oxytocin.R states. Independent data show oxytocin metabolic clearance is the same in pregnant and nonpregnant subjects: Leake 1980 (constant infusion 4 mU/min, n=22) MCR 23.1 (pregnant at term, induction) vs 20.6 (nonpregnant women) vs 27 ml/kg/min (men); Takeda 1989 (n=14) 20.9-22.1 (pregnant 38-41 wk) vs 19.7-22.7 ml/kg/min (nonpregnant). Placental oxytocinase (cystine aminopeptidase) degrades oxytocin in vitro but does not measurably raise in vivo clearance.
source: Leake RD, Weitzman RE, Fisher DA. Pharmacokinetics of oxytocin in the human subject. Obstet Gynecol 1980;56:701-4 PMID 7443113; Takeda S, Kuwabara Y, Mizuno M. [Metabolic clearance rate of oxytocin in human subjects]. Nihon Naibunpi Gakkai Zasshi 1989;65:182-9 PMID 2767286
notes: The model's source is unpublished (help page calls it one of the two weakest citations in the library); its parturient population is stated in the code comment only.

finding: The library applies elimination CL x3.8/2.6 = 1.46 (Ansari 2016, citing Kokki 2012: labouring-women elimination half-time 2.6 h vs non-pregnant 3.8 h). Kokki 2012 (n=15 nulliparous, 1 mg IV boluses in first-stage labour) reported maternal half-life 2.6 h (1.8-2.8), 'significantly shorter than that reported in non-pregnant women'. Oxycodone is cleared by CYP3A4 (noroxycodone) and CYP2D6 (oxymorphone), both induced, plus the GFR rise; the review attributes the faster clearance to all three. The 2018 Clin Pharmacokinet review (Kinnunen) summarises the same.
applied: Elimination clearance × 3.8/2.6 = 1.46; volumes and oxymorphone formation unchanged.
source: Kokki M, Franco MG, Raatikainen K, et al. Basic Clin Pharmacol Toxicol 2012;111:182-188 PMID 22448718; Kinnunen M, Piirainen P, Kokki H, et al. Clin Pharmacokinet 2019;58:705-725 PMID 30652261
notes: No change indicated. Oxymorphone formation (CYP2D6, induced) left unchanged as the review gives no metabolite figure; the model header already states this. Total plasma plotted.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. The only obstetric-adjacent data are a PBPK breast-milk/relative-infant-dose simulation after cesarean (Ding 2026) that assumes adult disposition and does not estimate a maternal pregnancy clearance change. Oliceridine is metabolized by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 (both induced in pregnancy), so clearance would plausibly rise in direction only.
source: Ding Y, Liu K, Zhang S, et al. J Clin Pharmacol 2026;66:e70228 PMID 42678308
notes: Investigational/newly approved; essentially no pregnancy literature. Total plasma plotted.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic data in pregnancy. Retrieved literature is narrative/focused reviews of obstetric use, a retrospective case series, and an in-vitro placental transporter (OATP2B1) study.
source: Chae R, Kearsley R, Lee A, Duffy C. Remimazolam in obstetric anaesthesia: a focused review. Int J Obstet Anesth 2025;65:104790 PMID 41092577
notes: Remimazolam is hydrolysed by hepatic carboxylesterase-1; pregnancy effects on CES1 are not characterised.

finding: Ridd 1989 (read in full): 5 women given 5 mg IV 1.5-3 h before caesarean section at 38-40 weeks, not in labour; in 4, free plasma clearance 42.5 (5.5) mL/min/kg, similar to nonpregnant women of comparable age; total plasma clearance (time-averaged) 0.94 (0.30) mL/min/kg, Varea 2.37 L/kg, half-life 30 h, mean free fraction 2.19%. Total and blood concentrations rose about 50% and 40% at delivery as the free fraction swung with the surgical rise in nonesterified fatty acids (r up to 0.89), so the total clearance reflects the operation's binding changes, not pregnancy. Jorgensen 1988: 66 first-trimester women, oral 10-25 mg, parameters within the normal adult range. Moore & McBride 1978 (read in full): 14 women given 10 mg IV within 10 h of delivery at 37-40 weeks with uneventful puerperia had a total plasma clearance of 28.2 ± 9.6 mL/min (blood clearance 43.8, blood/plasma ratio 0.62), against 26-35 mL/min in four nonpregnant series; the terminal half-life was longer (65 vs 29-34 h), which the authors attribute to postnatal redistribution of diazepam into the maternal circulation (a 50% rise in concentration within 18 h of delivery), not to a change in elimination. Four women with tubal ligation the next day cleared 56 mL/min with a 31 h half-life.
source: Ridd MJ, Brown KF, Nation RL, Collier CB. The disposition and placental transfer of diazepam in cesarean section. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1989;45:506-512 PMID 2721106; Jorgensen NP, Thurmann-Nielsen E, Walstad RA. Pharmacokinetics and distribution of diazepam and oxazepam in early pregnancy. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand 1988;67:493-497 PMID 3239381; Moore RG, McBride WG. The disposition kinetics of diazepam in pregnant women at parturition. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1978;13:275-284 PMID 668785
notes: The library plots TOTAL diazepam. If fu rises in pregnancy (albumin falls ~20%) with unchanged unbound clearance, total clearance and Vss would rise roughly in proportion to fu, but no fu ratio was retrieved for diazepam. Placental UV/MV total 1.73, free 0.92 (Ridd). The longer half-life at term (Moore & McBride) is a redistribution around delivery, not a steady change the model could carry: clearance, the quantity the flag would scale, is unchanged.

finding: Papini 2005 (read in full): 10 term parturients (36-40 weeks, in labour), single 2 mg oral dose, 48 h sampling, two-compartment fit: CL/F 2.6 mL/min/kg (95% CI 2.3-2.9), Vd/F 178.8 L, t1/2 10.4 h, ke 0.068 /h; the authors conclude that pregnancy increases apparent oral clearance and distribution volume and shortens the half-life. No non-pregnant arm; comparison is against this library's own non-pregnant model (Nielsen-Kudsk 1983: CL 62.17 mL/kg/h IV, Vd-area 1.24 L/kg, t1/2 14.1 h; oral F 0.90). Not applied: the only parturient study (Papini 2005) has no nonpregnant arm; its ratios (CL/F × 2.26, V/F × 1.67) are against this library's own model.
comparator: historical non-pregnant volunteers (this library's Nielsen-Kudsk 1983 model)
source: Papini O, da Cunha SP, da Silva Mathes Ado C, et al. Kinetic disposition of lorazepam with focus on the glucuronidation capacity, transplacental transfer in parturients and racemization in biological samples. J Pharm Biomed Anal 2005;40:397-403 PMID 16143486
notes: Mechanism: lorazepam is cleared by UGT2B15 glucuronidation; pregnancy induces UGTs (e.g. lamotrigine). Oral bioavailability in labour is unknown; the factor is on CL/F and is applied to IV/IM clearance by assumption. Total concentrations. Per-kg comparison: the library already scales with fat-free mass at the entered (pregnant) weight, so applying per-kg factors on top slightly undercounts the pregnant weight's contribution; acceptable within the uncertainty. Not in Ansari 2016.

finding: No pregnancy pharmacokinetic study (pregnant vs non-pregnant or postpartum) was found in PubMed. Alprazolam is a CYP3A4 substrate; Hebert 2008 (midazolam) suggests CL/F would rise in late pregnancy but no alprazolam data exist (Yamamoto 2019 used Simcyp's pregnancy population to predict a single case, no ratio reported).
source: Yamamoto K, Fukushima S, Mishima Y, et al. Pharmacokinetic assessment of alprazolam-induced neonatal abstinence syndrome using physiologically based pharmacokinetic model. Drug Metab Pharmacokinet 2019;34:400-402 PMID 31699653
notes: Do not borrow midazolam's or lorazepam's factor without drug-specific evidence; record as unknown on the help page.

finding: No pregnancy pharmacokinetic study (pregnant vs non-pregnant or postpartum) was found in PubMed. Clonazepam is cleared by CYP3A4 nitroreduction; no pregnancy PK study found.
notes: Do not borrow midazolam's or lorazepam's factor without drug-specific evidence; record as unknown on the help page.

finding: No pregnancy pharmacokinetic study (pregnant vs non-pregnant or postpartum) was found in PubMed. Zolpidem is ~60% CYP3A4; studies retrieved are placental transfer only (Juric 2009 cord/maternal 0.48-2.75 in 6 pairs; Saito 2022 case series).
source: Juric S, Newport DJ, Ritchie JC, Galanti M, Stowe ZN. Zolpidem (Ambien) in pregnancy: placental passage and outcome. Arch Womens Ment Health 2009;12:441-446 PMID 19657707
notes: Do not borrow midazolam's or lorazepam's factor without drug-specific evidence; record as unknown on the help page.

finding: No pregnancy pharmacokinetic study (pregnant vs non-pregnant or postpartum) was found in PubMed. Temazepam is cleared by direct glucuronidation (UGT2B7/2B15), which pregnancy may induce (compare lorazepam), but the only retrieved study is placental transfer at 12-17 weeks (Cooper 2001: fetal:maternal 0.38).
source: Cooper J, Jauniaux E, Gulbis B, Bromley L. Placental transfer of temazepam and fentanyl in early human pregnancy. Reprod Biomed Online 2001;2:165-171 PMID 12537792
notes: Do not borrow midazolam's or lorazepam's factor without drug-specific evidence; record as unknown on the help page.

finding: The library models codeine as a prodrug whose analgesia is formed morphine via a CYP2D6-scaled formation clearance (phenotype-weighted), with the effect shown on the morphine row. CYP2D6 is induced in pregnancy: Tracy 2005 (paired phenotyping, n=25) found CYP2D6 activity increased 25.6% at 14-18 wk, 34.8% at 24-28 wk and 47.8% at 36-40 wk vs postpartum; Wadelius 1997 confirmed induction in extensive metabolisers. Badaoui 2021 PBPK predicts higher fetal morphine exposure in CYP2D6 ultrarapid mothers. Ansari 2016 states only direction (faster morphine formation, higher peak), no magnitude; the library row is 'unquantified'.
source: Tracy TS, Venkataramanan R, Glover DD, Caritis SN. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2005;192:633-639 PMID 15696014; Wadelius M, Darj E, Frenne G, Rane A. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1997;62:400-407 PMID 9357391; Badaoui S, Hopkins AM, Rodrigues AD, et al. AAPS J 2021;23:15 PMID 33404848
notes: The morphine formed is plotted on the morphine row (total plasma). The CYP2D6 rise is a general probe result, not codeine-specific; if applied it should scale the formation branch only, and codeine is given cyp2d6 phenotype already, so pregnancy would act on top of phenotype. Morphine clearance itself also rises (see morphine row), which partly offsets higher formation.

finding: No human pregnancy PK study. Hydrocodone is carried as apparent oral parameters (CL/F, Vc/F) and forms hydromorphone via CYP2D6 (and noroxycodone-type metabolites via CYP3A4). Both CYP2D6 (+26-48%, Tracy 2005) and CYP3A4 (+35-38%) are induced in pregnancy, so apparent clearance would rise and hydromorphone formation increase; Ansari 2016 gives direction only ('increased CYP2D6 activity increases conversion to hydromorphone'), which the library encodes as 'unquantified'. The only obstetric data (Stauble 2013, post-cesarean CYP2D6 genotype; Sauberan 2011 breast milk) are postpartum and do not give a pregnancy clearance ratio.
source: Tracy TS, Venkataramanan R, Glover DD, Caritis SN. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2005;192:633-639 PMID 15696014; Stauble ME, Moore AW, Langman LJ, et al. Clin Chim Acta 2013;429:26-29 PMID 24269714
notes: Apparent-oral model; total plasma plotted; hydromorphone metabolite calibrated to an observed ratio, not a formation flux, so a pregnancy formation factor cannot be cleanly inserted. Matches the library's existing 'unquantified' row.

finding: No human pregnancy PK study for oxymorphone as a drug or as oxycodone's metabolite. Oxymorphone is carried as a one-compartment apparent-oral model (no human central volume exists) and as oxycodone's active metabolite. It is cleared by UGT (3- and 6-glucuronidation) and some CYP3A; no pregnancy-specific clearance data were found. Sheep data (Kinnunen 2018/2019) show oxymorphone accumulation in the fetus after maternal oxycodone but give no maternal human factor.
source: Kinnunen M, Kokki H, Hautajarvi H, et al. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand 2018;97:1200-1205 PMID 29772054
notes: Oxymorphone formation from oxycodone is set in R/drugs_oxycodone.R and left unchanged by the oxycodone pregnancy factor; that is consistent with leaving oxymorphone's own disposition unchanged. Total plasma plotted.

finding: Strong, consistent new evidence that dose-normalized buprenorphine exposure is substantially lower in pregnancy, i.e. apparent clearance is higher. Bastian/Caritis 2016 (n=13-14 sublingual, within-woman pregnancy vs postpartum) found dose-normalized AUC ~50% lower during pregnancy than postpartum (AUC p<0.003, Cmax p<0.018). Zhu/Caritis 2024 (n=22, 33 studies) found dose-normalized AUC 155 vs 218 ng*min/mL (pregnancy vs postpartum, ratio 1.41 overall) and 119 vs 218 in the second half of pregnancy (ratio 1.83). Mechanism (PMID 31929398): pregnancy increases CYP3A N-demethylation and UGT glucuronidation of buprenorphine. A validated PBPK (Zhu 2018) reproduces the lower exposure. The library row is currently 'unquantified' (direction only).
applied: Elimination clearance × 218/119 = 1.83 (Zhu 2024, second half of pregnancy against postpartum); volumes and the sublingual and intranasal absorption unchanged.
design: paired NCA / popPK (sublingual) + mechanistic metabolism + PBPK
source: Bastian JR, Chen H, Zhang H, et al. (Caritis group) Am J Obstet Gynecol 2017;216:64.e1-64.e7 PMID 27687214; Caritis SN, Bastian JR, Zhang H, et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2017;217:459.e1-459.e6 PMID 28669739; Zhu Y, Bastian JR, Caritis SN, et al. J Addict Med 2024;19:129-134 PMID 39221812; Liu Y, et al. (Venkataramanan group) Ther Drug Monit 2020;42:264-270 (Pregnancy Alters CYP- and UGT-Mediated Metabolism of Buprenorphine) PMID 31929398; Zhang H, Kalluri HV, Bastian JR, et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2018;84:2075-2087 (PBPK) PMID 29873094
notes: The pregnancy data are apparent (sublingual CL/F), but the mechanistic study (PMID 31929398) attributes the lower exposure to increased CYP3A/UGT metabolism (clearance), not reduced absorption, and Tmax/pH were unchanged, so applying the factor to the absolute elimination clearance cl1 (rather than to F) is the correct mapping for the library's absolute Bjornsson disposition. Total plasma buprenorphine plotted (norbuprenorphine not modelled). The library's help pregnancy table currently reads 'Increased metabolism ... a dose increase is needed in the third trimester. No magnitude is given.' - that row should be revised to a quantified entry.

finding: The library models tramadol as a prodrug, showing only the mu-opioid activity of its CYP2D6-formed metabolite desmetramadol on the desmetramadol row. CYP2D6 is induced in pregnancy (Tracy 2005, +26-48% across trimesters), so desmetramadol formation would increase and parent clearance rise; tramadol is also cleared by CYP3A4 and renally. No pregnant-vs-nonpregnant tramadol clearance ratio was found: obstetric data are labour/placental (Claahsen 2005: maternal terminal t1/2 7.2 h, no non-pregnant comparator) and postpartum breast-milk popPK (Salman 2011).
design: physiological (CYP2D6 probe); labour NCA; postpartum popPK
source: Tracy TS, Venkataramanan R, Glover DD, Caritis SN. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2005;192:633-639 PMID 15696014; Claahsen-van der Grinten HL, Verbruggen I, van den Berg PP, et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2005;61:523-529 PMID 16007420; Salman S, Sy SKB, Ilett KF, et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2011;67:899-908 PMID 21394525
notes: Desmetramadol (O-desmethyltramadol) is the row that carries the opioid effect (total plasma). Parent tramadol is not fully described by the opioid model anyway (monoaminergic action out of scope), so a pregnancy factor would act only on the CYP2D6 formation branch if applied at all.

finding: No antepartum gabapentin PK study was found. Silvola 2025 (popPK, n=20, 300 mg PO q6h started before cesarean, PK dose sampled in the first 48 h postpartum) estimated CL/F 15.6 L/h and V/F 284 L, which the authors compare with 14-15 L/h and 58 L in healthy volunteers (median eGFR 151 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 107.5 kg); covariates could not be tested and the V/F is driven by a constrained ka (flip-flop), so it is not usable. Arfman 2020 (review of AED TDM in pregnancy) finds 'inadequate or no evidence' for changes in gabapentin clearance. Gabapentin is eliminated unchanged by the kidney. Not applied: the general rise in filtration would give × 1.5, but the one peripartum study (Silvola 2025) found CL/F only 4-11% above healthy volunteers.
source: Silvola R et al. Population pharmacokinetics and transfer of gabapentin when used as a pain adjunct for cesarean deliveries. CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2025;14:551-560 PMID 39891423; Arfman IJ et al. Therapeutic drug monitoring of antiepileptic drugs in women with epilepsy before, during, and after pregnancy. Clin Pharmacokinet 2020;59:427-445 PMID 31912315
notes: Total = unbound (<3% bound). Silvola's PK dose was postpartum, so it is not a late-pregnancy estimate; it also mixes F (saturable absorption) into CL/F. Renal term is Cockcroft-Gault on the entered weight and creatinine. If the user enters the pregnant woman's ACTUAL serum creatinine (typically 0.4-0.6 mg/dL at term) and actual weight, CG already reports much of the GFR rise, and multiplying by 1.5 double-counts. The 1.5 factor is cleanest when the creatinine field is blank (assumed normal nonpregnant creatinine); the library applies one policy for all renal drugs (cefazolin/gentamicin/vancomycin already multiply unconditionally).

finding: No PK study in pregnancy found; Tomson 2013 (Epilepsia review) states pregnancy PK data are 'lacking completely' for pregabalin. In lactating women >=12 weeks postpartum (Lockwood 2016, n=10, 150 mg q12h) ~89% of the dose was recovered in urine, renal clearance 68.2 mL/min, and lactation had little influence on PK. Pregabalin is cleared almost entirely unchanged by glomerular filtration. Not applied: the model caps renal function at a normalised creatinine clearance of 96.4, so a 1.5-fold filtration rise has no effect in a woman with normal renal function.
source: Tomson T, Landmark CJ, Battino D. Antiepileptic drug treatment in pregnancy: changes in drug disposition and their clinical implications. Epilepsia 2013;54:405-14 PMID 23360413; Lockwood PA et al. The pharmacokinetics of pregabalin in breast milk, plasma, and urine of healthy postpartum women. J Hum Lact 2016;32:NP1-NP8 PMID 26961752
notes: Not protein bound (total = unbound). Renal term is Cockcroft-Gault on the entered weight and creatinine. If the user enters the pregnant woman's ACTUAL serum creatinine (typically 0.4-0.6 mg/dL at term) and actual weight, CG already reports much of the GFR rise, and multiplying by 1.5 double-counts. The 1.5 factor is cleanest when the creatinine field is blank (assumed normal nonpregnant creatinine); the library applies one policy for all renal drugs (cefazolin/gentamicin/vancomycin already multiply unconditionally).

finding: IV paracetamol at cesarean delivery: median CL 11.9 L/h/m2 vs 8.4 in nonpregnant women and 6.42 postpartum (Beleyn 2014, single 2 g IV); paired (n=8) delivery vs 10-15 wk postpartum 22.19 vs 11.31 L/h (11.7 vs 6.4 L/h/m2, Kulo 2012 J Biomed Biotechnol); popPK (Kulo 2013, read in full, 39 women) total CL 21.1 vs 11.7 L/h postpartum (disproportional rise in glucuronidation; V1 50.2 L, the volume increase not reliably estimable); pooled popPK (Allegaert 2015, read in full, n=69) glucuronidation CL x2.03 at delivery (14.9 vs 7.33 L/h vs healthy nonpregnant volunteers), sulfation unchanged, net total clearance ~1.6x; central volume V1 x1.86 (34.4 vs 18.5 L, weight-standardised) is a central-compartment term NOT applied, since Kulo 2014's steady-state volume per kg was unchanged (0.69 vs 0.74 L/kg). Early postpartum is itself LOW (glucuronidation x0.55), so paired postpartum ratios (~1.8-2.0) overstate the change vs a nonpregnant reference. Kulo 2014 (read in full, pooled n=73) agrees: delivery CL 11.7 vs 6.4 L/h/m2 (BSA; +80% unnormalised, glucuronidation-driven) and distribution volume 56 vs ~46 L but 0.69 vs 0.74 L/kg, i.e. unchanged per kg. Oral, third trimester (Miners 1986, read in full; 8 women at 31-38 weeks, 68 kg, against 12 nonpregnant women, 63 kg; saliva): CL/F 27.10 vs 17.12 L/h (1.58), half-life 1.52 vs 2.11 h, so V/F 1.14 times; glucuronidation 1.75 and oxidation 1.88 times, sulphation and renal clearance unchanged; the two women at 38 weeks had the lowest clearances (20.1 and 21.6 L/h, 1.22 times). Rayburn 1986 (n=6, oral, 36 wk vs 6 wk postpartum) found no significant difference, the basis of the 'unchanged' statement in Ansari 2016.
applied: Clearance × 1.5 and both volumes × 1.14; absorption unchanged. (CL raised from 1.4 after reading Allegaert 2015 in full: the cross-sectional nonpregnant comparisons Beleyn 1.42, Miners 1.58 and Allegaert net ~1.6 give a median ~1.58, tempered to 1.5. Allegaert's central-volume 1.86 is not applied.)
source: Allegaert K et al. Paracetamol pharmacokinetics and metabolism in young women. BMC Anesthesiol 2015;15:163 PMID 26566962; Beleyn B et al. Estradiol and weight are covariates of paracetamol clearance in young women. Gynecol Obstet Invest 2014 PMID 24686129; Kulo A et al. The impact of caesarean delivery on paracetamol and ketorolac pharmacokinetics: a paired analysis. J Biomed Biotechnol 2012;2012:437639 PMID 22675252; Kulo A et al. Pharmacokinetics of paracetamol and its metabolites in women at delivery and post-partum. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2013;75:850-60 PMID 22845052; Miners JO, Robson RA, Birkett DJ. Paracetamol metabolism in pregnancy. Br J Clin Pharmacol 1986;22:359-62 PMID 3768250; Rayburn W et al. Acetaminophen pharmacokinetics: comparison between pregnant and nonpregnant women. Am J Obstet Gynecol 1986;155:1353-6 PMID 3789044; Allegaert K et al. The pharmacokinetics of a high intravenous dose of paracetamol after caesarean delivery: the effect of gestational age. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2012;29:484-8 PMID 22935956; Kulo A et al. Pharmacokinetics of a loading dose of intravenous paracetamol post caesarean delivery. Int J Obstet Anesth 2012;21:125-8 PMID 22341787
notes: Conflicts with the current pregnancyFindings() row ('unchanged', from Ansari 2016, which rests on Rayburn's n=6 oral study); the IV delivery data and Miners are larger and consistent. Data are immediately post-cesarean (hours after delivery), i.e. the end of pregnancy, plus surgery. Postpartum (10-15 wk) clearance is BELOW nonpregnant values, so do not use paired ratios against Morse. Total plasma concentration; paracetamol binding is low, so total ~ unbound. The effect-site model (Anderson 2001) is unaffected.

finding: No human study of ibuprofen pharmacokinetics in pregnancy or at delivery was found (searches for pregnancy/postpartum/cesarean/tocolysis returned only neonatal PDA, milk-transfer and rodent/veterinary studies). An in vitro hepatocyte study found third-trimester hormone concentrations did not change CYP2C9 activity (diclofenac probe).
source: Alshabi A et al. A cocktail probe approach to evaluate the effect of hormones on the expression and activity of CYP enzymes in human hepatocytes with conditions simulating late stage of pregnancy. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2023;79:815-827 PMID 37060457
notes: Highly albumin bound: a fall in albumin would raise the unbound fraction and lower total concentrations, unquantified. The library plots total racemic ibuprofen.

finding: No human pregnancy or post-cesarean PK study of diclofenac found (search returned efficacy trials and placental perfusion/PK-PD predictions using nonpregnant parameters). In vitro, third-trimester hormone concentrations did not alter CYP2C9-mediated diclofenac metabolism in human hepatocytes (Alshabi 2023).
source: Alshabi A et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2023;79:815-827 PMID 37060457; Shintaku K et al. Prediction and evaluation of fetal toxicity induced by NSAIDs using transplacental kinetic parameters obtained from human placental perfusion studies. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2012;73:248-56 PMID 21261677
notes: Model is Standing 2011 (children + adult oral data); total plasma. Highly albumin bound.

finding: Same as diclofenac: no human pregnancy PK data for any diclofenac formulation found.
source: Alshabi A et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2023;79:815-827 PMID 37060457
notes: Apparent (/F) parameters; any change in F or CL is unidentifiable without data.

finding: No human pregnancy or postpartum PK study of meloxicam found (only dairy-cattle and goat postpartum/lactation studies).
notes: Total plasma; >99% albumin bound, so the free fraction may rise in pregnancy (unquantified). The cyp2c9 covariate stays as is.

finding: Racemic IV ketorolac 30 mg at cesarean delivery (Kulo 2012 IJOA, read in full, n=39; 8 re-studied 4-5 months postpartum; 8 nonpregnant controls): CL 2.11 vs 1.43 (late postpartum) and 1.07 L/h/m2 (controls), i.e. absolute CL 3.92 vs 1.82 L/h against controls (weights 76 vs 63 kg); V 0.24 vs 0.16 and 0.17 L/kg. Paired (n=8, Kulo 2012 J Biomed Biotechnol): CL 3.80 vs 2.53 L/h (2.03 vs 1.43 L/h/m2). Late-postpartum CL (1.43 L/h/m2) equals healthy men (1.48). Enantiomer-specific NCA (Kulo 2017, read in full, same cohort, delivery n=31 vs 8 healthy female volunteers): BSA/weight-normalised, S-ketorolac CL/BSA 3.47/2.06 = 1.68 and Vss/BW 0.18/0.15 = 1.20; R-ketorolac CL/BSA 1.18/0.59 = 2.00 and Vss/BW 0.12/0.09 = 1.33; CL rises more than Vss, so the terminal half-life is numerically shorter at delivery (not significant, n=8).
applied: Enantiomer-specific (Kulo 2017): S-ketorolac elimination clearance × 1.68 and volumes × 1.20, R-ketorolac elimination clearance × 2.00 and volumes × 1.33; the distribution clearances scale with volume, so the distribution phase is unchanged and the terminal half-life shortens slightly. (The registry cl/v_factor record the S enantiomer, which the generic test checks on cl1/v1; the R factors are checked by a dedicated test.)
comparator: healthy female volunteers (Kulo 2017); same women 4-5 months postpartum (paired)
source: Kulo A et al. Pharmacokinetics of intravenous ketorolac following caesarean delivery. Int J Obstet Anesth 2012;21:334-8 PMID 22901775; Kulo A et al. The impact of caesarean delivery on paracetamol and ketorolac pharmacokinetics: a paired analysis. J Biomed Biotechnol 2012;2012:437639 PMID 22675252; Kulo A et al. Enantiomer-specific ketorolac pharmacokinetics in young women, including pregnancy and postpartum period. Bosn J Basic Med Sci 2017;17:54-60 PMID 27968707; Cloesmeijer ME et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2021;87:1443-1454 (the library's source model) PMID 32901947
notes: Model plots total S+R ketorolac. Ketorolac is highly albumin bound; part of the higher CL and V at delivery may be a higher free fraction (fall in albumin), in which case UNBOUND concentrations change less than total. Kulo notes surgical stress may also contribute. Cloesmeijer's adult data include the Leuven late-postpartum women, which is why that group is the comparator.

finding: No naproxen PK study in pregnant women found. R/pregnancy.R notes that Ansari 2016 mentions naproxen only in its text (no factor in its tables); that text was not retrieved here.
notes: Apparent oral model (Valitalo 2012, re-centred). >99% albumin bound: free fraction likely rises with hypoalbuminaemia of pregnancy (unquantified); the library plots total.

finding: No celecoxib PK study in pregnancy found (searched with the other NSAIDs). CYP2C9 substrate; in vitro third-trimester hormones did not change CYP2C9 activity (Alshabi 2023).
source: Alshabi A et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2023;79:815-827 PMID 37060457
notes: Apparent oral parameters fitted to a mean curve; total plasma.

finding: Shanmugalingam 2019 (read in full; 12 high-risk pregnant women in four groups of 3 vs 3 nonpregnant women, salicylic acid measured): with 100 mg aspirin, salicylic acid CL +44% +/- 8% (P<0.01) and AUC0-24 lower in pregnancy vs nonpregnant; 150 mg restored the pregnant 24-h AUC toward the nonpregnant 100 mg value; the 48% +/- 1% higher volume and 4-h Tmax delay were an enteric-coated vs non-enteric-coated preparation effect, not pregnancy, and morning vs evening dosing did not differ. A pregnancy PBPK model (Collins-Smith 2026) predicts salicylic acid AUC falling ~20% at 10 weeks and ~30% at 40 weeks (1/0.70 = 1.43-fold CL). No data for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) itself. Ansari 2016 (per R/pregnancy.R) reports only slower uptake and a lower peak, no magnitude. Not applied: salicylate clearance +44% rests on 3 nonpregnant controls (a PBPK model predicts × 1.43).
trimester: not stated in abstract (high-risk women on prophylaxis, typically 2nd-3rd trimester)
comparator: nonpregnant women (n=3, crossover in the controls only)
source: Shanmugalingam R et al. A pharmacokinetic assessment of optimal dosing, preparation, and chronotherapy of aspirin in pregnancy. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2019;221:255.e1-255.e9 PMID 31051121; Collins-Smith A et al. Development of a pregnancy-specific physiologically based pharmacokinetics (PBPK) model for aspirin. CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2026;15:e70130 PMID 41574863
notes: The library plots ASA (antiplatelet species); the measured change is in salicylic acid, its metabolite. AUC -40% exceeds the +44% CL effect alone (1/1.44 = 0.69), so part may be lower F or larger V. Changes pregnancyFindings() from 'unquantified' to quantified for salicylate only.

finding: Philipson 1987 (read in full; 6 women at 19-33 weeks, IV 0.5 g during and after pregnancy, bioassay): total clearance 7.30 vs 4.66 L/h (x1.57, not significant), half-life 1.12 vs 1.72 h (x0.65, P < 0.005), volume 11.7 vs 11.6 L. Total cefazolin clearance is higher in late pregnancy. In a paired study (6 women, IV, during vs after pregnancy) the AUC was 31% smaller and the half-life 35% shorter in pregnancy (Philipson 1987): CL ratio 1/(1-0.31) = 1.45, and V ratio about 1.45 x 0.65 = 0.94, i.e. volume essentially unchanged. In 20 parturients at caesarean, clearance before delivery was 7.18 L/h against 4.12 L/h after delivery (Elkomy 2014, read in full; one-compartment, V 9.44 L): 7.18/4.12 = 1.74, though 'after delivery' is hours postpartum, not a non-pregnant baseline. Allegaert 2009 (read in full; 82 pregnancies, 17-40 weeks, popPK; clearance almost exclusively renal) gave CL 7.44 L/h (about twice healthy young adults' 3.6 L/h) and V 12.04 L with no gestational-age trend; Popovic 2007 (primary table read in full) found no significant pregnant-vs-non-pregnant difference in cefazolin (ke 0.1095 vs 0.1113 /h, essentially identical; non-pregnant n=4). van Hasselt 2014 explained the gestational effect entirely through the rise in creatinine clearance.
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the published renal term when the serum creatinine is left blank, so unbound clearance × 1.27; volumes unchanged. A measured creatinine already carries the rise.
trimester: third (term, caesarean); paired study across pregnancy
comparator: same women after pregnancy (Philipson); same women hours after delivery (Elkomy)
source: Philipson A, Stiernstedt G, Ehrnebo M. Comparison of the pharmacokinetics of cephradine and cefazolin in pregnant and non-pregnant women. Clin Pharmacokinet 1987;12:136-44 PMID 3829560; Elkomy MH et al. Pharmacokinetics of prophylactic cefazolin in parturients undergoing cesarean delivery. Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2014;58:3504-13 PMID 24733461; Allegaert K et al. Cefazolin pharmacokinetics in maternal plasma and amniotic fluid during pregnancy. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2009;200:170.e1-7 PMID 19006783; van Hasselt JG et al. Semiphysiological versus empirical modelling of the population pharmacokinetics of free and total cefazolin during pregnancy. Biomed Res Int 2014;2014:897216 PMID 24672799; Popovic J, Grujic Z, Sabo A. Influence of pregnancy on ceftriaxone, cefazolin and gentamicin pharmacokinetics in caesarean vs. non-pregnant sectioned women. J Clin Pharm Ther 2007;32:595-602 PMID 18021337
notes: IMPORTANT for all three renal antibiotics: the 1.5 factor stands in for the hyperfiltration of pregnancy that a NON-PREGNANT serum creatinine cannot show. If the user enters the parturient's own measured creatinine (typically 0.4-0.6 mg/dL), Cockcroft-Gault already reports the higher filtration, and multiplying again double-counts it (see the vancomycin entry, where a model fitted to measured pregnant creatinine needed no extra factor). Recommend applying PREGNANCY_GFR_FACTOR only when creatinine is NULL (assumed). The model plots UNBOUND cefazolin; the unbound fraction rises in pregnancy (albumin falls about 15%), so total concentrations fall more than the plotted unbound curve does. The PBPK models (Abduljalil 2022; Dallmann 2017) reproduce the pregnancy data but were not used for numbers.

finding: Muller 2010 (read in full; 7 peripartum women, mean 86 kg, 3 of them with endocarditis) fitted a three-compartment popPK model: CL 10.0 L/h (95% CI 2.65-17.35, CV 37.5%), gamma half-life 2.6 h, and a Vss reported as 6.32 x 10^3 L (6320 L) -- implausibly large, so the disposition volumes are poorly identified from the sparse peripartum sampling. Groen 2023 notes this clearance is LOWER than literature values in non-pregnant adults (19.8-26.4 L/h), and the library's own Bouazza 2012 value is 15.2 L/h (cross-study ratio 10.0/15.2 = 0.66). The Ansari review describes a 'decreased AUC/MIC ratio' (i.e. faster clearance) without a magnitude. The two directions conflict and neither is a within-study comparison.
source: Muller AE et al. Pharmacokinetics of clindamycin in pregnant women in the peripartum period. Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2010;54:2175-81 PMID 20176904; Groen F et al. Clin Pharmacokinet 2023;62:399-434 PMID 36940039
notes: Clindamycin is AAG-bound (saturable); AAG falls in pregnancy, so the unbound fraction should rise, which would raise total clearance, the opposite of Muller's estimate. Hepatic CYP3A4 (its main pathway) is induced in pregnancy. Without a controlled comparison, no factor is defensible.

finding: Philipson 1987 (read in full): cephradine, the analogue, in 12 women during (weeks 10-29) and after pregnancy: IV clearance 22.4 vs 14.1 L/h (x1.59, P < 0.001), falling with gestational week per kg; in the three women studied at 24 weeks or later the absolute ratios were 1.69, 1.47 and 1.35 (geometric mean 1.50); oral bioavailability 105% vs 85%, not different. No pregnancy PK study of cefalexin with a non-pregnant comparator was found (Creatsas 1980 measured serum and amniotic levels after 1 g PO in 60 pregnant women without a control). The closest analogue, cephradine (oral, renally cleared, low binding, near-identical structure), was studied paired during and after pregnancy in 12 women: IV AUC 39% smaller (CL ratio 1/(1-0.39) = 1.64), half-life 26% shorter (V ratio 1.64 x 0.74 = 1.21), and oral bioavailability unchanged (Philipson 1987). Cefalexin itself is 70-100% excreted unchanged in urine (Griffith 1983).
applied: CL/F × 1.5 (by analogy: cephradine's paired clearance ratio 1.64 and the 50% rise in filtration; no cefalexin data); V/F and absorption unchanged.
source: Philipson A, Stiernstedt G, Ehrnebo M. Clin Pharmacokinet 1987;12:136-44 PMID 3829560; Griffith RS. The pharmacology of cephalexin. Postgrad Med J 1983;59 Suppl 5:16-27 PMID 6364086; Creatsas G et al. A study of the kinetics of cephapirin and cephalexin in pregnancy. Curr Med Res Opin 1980;7:43-6 PMID 7428412
notes: The model is pediatric-origin apparent oral (CL/F, V/F); bioavailability is carried as 1 inside the apparent scale, so a pregnancy change in F (none expected) would also be a CL/F change. This is an analogue extrapolation, labelled as such.

finding: Evidence conflicts and is weak. Popovic 2007 (caesarean women vs non-pregnant gynaecological patients, one-compartment NCA) reported the ceftriaxone elimination rate constant significantly DECREASED in pregnancy (primary table read in full: ke 0.1109 vs 0.1817 /h, total clearance 24.4 vs 48.2 L/h). Grujic 2010 measured higher post-operative ceftriaxone concentrations after 2 g in 45 pregnant than in 4 non-pregnant women. A PBPK model (Chen 2026, Open Systems Pharmacology, calibrated to pregnancy data) predicts a 17% lower AUC (CL ratio 1/0.83 = 1.20) and 38% lower trough at 35 weeks. The Ansari review lists ceftriaxone as not significantly altered.
comparator: non-pregnant women (different subjects); PBPK non-pregnant adults
source: Chen et al. Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling and Pharmacodynamic Target Attainment Analysis for Ceftriaxone Dosing in Pregnant Women. J Clin Pharmacol 2026;66:e70205 PMID 42130310; Popovic J, Grujic Z, Sabo A. J Clin Pharm Ther 2007;32:595-602 PMID 18021337; Grujic Z et al. Preoperative administration of cephalosporins for elective caesarean delivery. Srp Arh Celok Lek 2010;138:600-3 PMID 21179910
to_obtain: Chen et al. J Clin Pharmacol 2026;66:e70205 (PMID 42130310): Gives which observed pregnancy data the PBPK model was calibrated to and the predicted CL and V separately; would decide whether CL x 1.2 is worth applying.
notes: Ceftriaxone is 85-95% albumin-bound with saturable binding; lower albumin in pregnancy raises the unbound fraction, which would raise total clearance and lower total concentrations, so the plotted TOTAL curve is the quantity most likely to fall. Mixed renal/biliary elimination, so the GFR factor alone is not appropriate.

finding: Goyal 2022 fitted a two-compartment popPK model to TDM data from 34 pregnant inpatients (2 first, 15 second, 17 third trimester; median creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, Cockcroft-Gault CrCL 176 mL/min computed from the pregnant creatinine without capping): CL 7.64 L/h x (CrCL/175) x (FFM/45), Vc 67.35 L, Q 9.06 L/h (fixed), Vp 37.5 L (fixed). Clearance at a given CrCL was close to the non-pregnant model, and the simulated AUC was the same (223 vs 226 mg.h/L). Check against this library's Thomson model: CL = 2.99 x [1 + 0.0154 x (175 - 66)] = 8.01 L/h at CrCL 175, against 7.64 L/h (ratio 0.95). With an assumed non-pregnant creatinine a 30-year-old 70 kg woman has CG CrCL of about (140-30) x 70 / (72 x 0.8) x 0.85 = 114 mL/min; x 1.5 = 170 mL/min, which is the CrCL the pregnant women actually had. Thomson's Vss at the cohort's median 74 kg is (0.675 + 0.732) x 74 = 104 L, against Goyal's 67.35 + 37.5 = 105 L.
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the published clearance term when the serum creatinine is left blank; volumes unchanged.
comparator: non-pregnant popPK model at the same CrCL and FFM
source: Goyal RK, Moffett BS, Gobburu JVS, Al Mohajer M. Population Pharmacokinetics of Vancomycin in Pregnant Women. Front Pharmacol 2022;13:873439 PMID 35734401; Groen F et al. Clin Pharmacokinet 2023;62:399-434 PMID 36940039
notes: This is the clearest evidence in the set that the 1.5 GFR factor and a measured pregnant creatinine are alternatives, not additions. Goyal's data are TDM troughs in hospitalised (often infected) women across all trimesters, with IIV estimable on CL only. Groen 2023 found no other vancomycin study with PK parameters and a non-pregnant comparison.

finding: Wang 2011 (read in full) studied 20 pregnant women with bacterial vaginosis (500 mg PO bid, steady state) at early, middle and late pregnancy: apparent oral CL/F 110 (middle) and 82 (late) mL/h/kg (about 7-9 L/h at 85 kg), with Vdss/F, CL/F and half-life not differing by stage and in the range of (slightly faster than) nonpregnant values. The Ansari review lists metronidazole as unchanged.
source: Wang X et al. Pharmacokinetics of metronidazole in pregnant patients with bacterial vaginosis. J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 2011;24:444-8 PMID 20608802
notes: Oral data only; the library model's IV disposition is untouched by this, and its oral F (0.841) is not contradicted.

finding: Lazebnik 1985 (read in full; 19 women at 28-34 weeks, 62 kg, against 17 nonpregnant women, 55 kg, 4 mg/kg/day): creatinine clearance 144.8 vs 96.3 mL/min (x1.50), serum creatinine 56.6 vs 74.3 umol/L, gentamicin half-life 93.5 vs 158.9 min (P < 0.0001), an elimination rate 1.70 times; half-life fell linearly with creatinine clearance. The one controlled study (18 third-trimester women at caesarean vs 4 non-pregnant women, 4 mg/kg IV, one-compartment NCA; Popovic 2007, primary table read in full) found the elimination rate constant higher in pregnancy (0.4127 vs 0.3198 /h, ratio 1.29) but total clearance only 5% higher (3.6 vs 3.41 L/h) and Vd 25% LOWER (9.05 vs 12.05 L); the heavier pregnant group received a larger weight-based dose, giving a higher Cmax. Lazebnik 1985 (19 women at 28-34 weeks vs 17 non-pregnant) found a significantly shorter half-life (numbers not in the abstract). Zaske 1980 (67 obstetric patients) found elimination poorly correlated with creatinine clearance (r=0.23) and dosing needs of 3.0-11.6 mg/kg/day. Postpartum TDM (Cropp 1998, n=28): Vd 0.29 L/kg dosing weight, ke 0.29 /h, half-life 2.5 h, CrCl 140 mL/min/1.73 m2.
applied: eGFR × 1.5 in the published renal term when the serum creatinine is left blank, so clearance × 1.5; volumes unchanged.
source: Groen F et al. The Pharmacokinetics and Target Attainment of Antimicrobial Drugs Throughout Pregnancy: Part III Non-penicillin and Non-cephalosporin Drugs. Clin Pharmacokinet 2023;62:399-434 PMID 36940039; Popovic J, Grujic Z, Sabo A. J Clin Pharm Ther 2007;32:595-602 PMID 18021337; Lazebnik N et al. Gentamicin serum half-life: a comparison between pregnant and non-pregnant women. Postgrad Med J 1985;61:979-81 PMID 4070116; Zaske DE et al. Rapid gentamicin elimination in obstetric patients. Obstet Gynecol 1980;56:559-64 PMID 7432725; Cropp CD et al. Evaluation of aminoglycoside pharmacokinetics in postpartum patients using Bayesian forecasting. Ther Drug Monit 1998;20:68-72 PMID 9485558
notes: Same caution as cefazolin: the factor must not be applied on top of a measured parturient creatinine. Groen 2023 concludes 'more robust studies are needed'. Smit 2020's ICU factor is not involved.

finding: No human study of exogenous hydrocortisone pharmacokinetics in pregnancy was found. The relevant physiological fact is binding: corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) rises 2- to 3-fold in normal pregnancy while albumin falls about 15% (as stated by Ryu 2018), which raises total cortisol and changes the bound/free partition. Pacheco 2007 (narrative review, read in full) confirms no quantified hydrocortisone pregnancy pharmacokinetics exist and notes hydrocortisone's nonlinear (saturable) protein binding.
source: Ryu RJ et al. Prednisone Pharmacokinetics During Pregnancy and Lactation. J Clin Pharmacol 2018;58:1223-1232 PMID 29733485; Pacheco LD et al. Pharmacokinetics of corticosteroids during pregnancy. Am J Perinatol 2007;24:79-82 PMID 17260328
notes: The model plots total cortisol above baseline; baseline total cortisol itself is 2-3x higher at term. Placental 11beta-HSD2 also inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Leave unchanged.

finding: No pharmacokinetic study of methylprednisolone in pregnant women was found; searches returned case reports (lupus nephritis, transplant, pemphigoid) and a breast-milk transfer report only.
source: Cooper SD et al. Transfer of methylprednisolone into breast milk in a mother with multiple sclerosis. J Hum Lact 2015;31:237-9 PMID 25691380
notes: Methylprednisolone is a CYP3A4 substrate that binds albumin but not CBG appreciably, so pregnancy would be expected to raise its clearance (CYP3A4 induction, higher unbound fraction); direction only.

finding: Tsuei 1980 (read in full; 8 mg dexamethasone phosphate IV, 5 women near term by caesarean, against 6 nonpregnant adults of their companion paper): total plasma clearance 559 vs 243 mL/min (x2.30), terminal half-life unchanged (mean 142 min, n = 10), protein binding unchanged (66.6% vs 68.1% bound). Because the half-life is unchanged while clearance doubles, the volume of distribution roughly doubles too; the authors attribute the rise to placental metabolism. Tsuei 1980 (term women at caesarean, 8 mg dexamethasone phosphate IV n=6 or IM n=6) found total plasma clearance 559 mL/min in pregnant against 243 mL/min in non-pregnant women (ratio 2.30) with an UNCHANGED terminal half-life (mean 142 min), which implies volume rose in proportion (about 2.3x); plasma binding was the same (66.6% vs 68.1% bound). Krzyzanski 2023 (hybrid minimal-PBPK meta-analysis of all parturient DEX and BET data) estimated maternal DEX clearance 26.7 L/h, against 9.5 L/h in non-pregnant (Indian) women from the same group (ratio 2.81), and a maternal tissue partition coefficient 2.37 vs 1.07 previously, i.e. a larger volume; IM absorption was faster (ka 0.893 vs 0.460 /h) and oral slower (0.446 vs 0.936 /h), F about 1. Against this library's Hong 2007 men (18.1 L/h) the absolute pregnant values are 33.5 L/h (Tsuei) and 26.7 L/h (Krzyzanski): 1.85 and 1.48.
applied: Elimination clearance × 2, both volumes × 2 and the distribution clearance × 2, so every rate constant and the terminal half-life are unchanged, as Tsuei 1980 measured.
comparator: non-pregnant women (Tsuei: different subjects; Krzyzanski: separate non-pregnant study by the same group)
source: Tsuei SE et al. Disposition of synthetic glucocorticoids. II. Dexamethasone in parturient women. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1980;28:88-98 PMID 7389259; Krzyzanski W, Milad MA, Jobe AH, Jusko WJ. Minimal physiologically-based hybrid model of pharmacokinetics in pregnant women: Application to antenatal corticosteroids. CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2023;12:668-680 PMID 36917704; Krzyzanski W et al. Cohort population analysis of sparse data: Dexamethasone pharmacokinetics in mother and fetus based on blood sampling at birth. J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn 2026 PMID 42406183; Egerman RS et al. A comparison of the bioavailability of oral and intramuscular dexamethasone in women in late pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol 1997;89:276-80 PMID 9015035
notes: The current x 2 is from Ansari ('clearance doubled in single gestation'); the primary data support it. Krzyzanski 2026 (J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn, read in full) is a Gauss-Hermite-quadrature estimation-methods paper using the birth-sampling dexamethasone data as a worked example; its one-compartment parameters are a methods demonstration, not a cleaner clinical factor, so the Tsuei-based x2/x2 stands. The half-life evidence (Tsuei) is the reason to add a volume factor; without it the simulated parturient curve falls about twice as fast as observed. Dose basis: Tsuei and Krzyzanski dosed dexamethasone phosphate, as the library does. Dexamethasone binding is NOT changed by pregnancy (Tsuei; Dean 1980 found its free fraction did not correlate with albumin), so total vs unbound is not an issue.

finding: Ryu 2018 studied 19 women on oral prednisone (4-40 mg/day) at steady state in early (n=3), mid (n=9) and late (n=14) pregnancy and postpartum (n=7; 6 women studied in both). UNBOUND prednisolone apparent clearance did not change with pregnancy. TOTAL prednisolone CL/F was lower in pregnancy (5 mg: 4.8 vs 11.3 L/h; 10 mg: 7.6 vs 7.6; 20 mg: 9.4 vs 11.6 L/h; 9.4/11.6 = 0.81), because the percent unbound was significantly lower in pregnancy (higher CBG). No gestational-age effect on total or unbound CL/F, half-life or V/F.
source: Ryu RJ et al. Prednisone Pharmacokinetics During Pregnancy and Lactation. J Clin Pharmacol 2018;58:1223-1232 PMID 29733485
notes: The paper's discussion says pregnancy 'increased' prednisolone CL/F, contradicting its own results section and abstract-level numbers (lower in pregnancy); the results numbers are used here. Total vs unbound matters: if the library ever switched to plotting TOTAL prednisolone, a factor of about 0.8 on total CL/F (higher CBG binding) would be indicated. Data are after oral PREDNISONE, not prednisolone, and the patients had lupus, RA etc.

finding: In the same study (Ryu 2018, 19 women, early/mid/late pregnancy vs postpartum), prednisone pharmacokinetic parameters did not differ significantly between pregnancy and postpartum; prednisone CL/F was dose-dependent (35.1, 52.6 and 64.3 L/h at 5, 10 and 20 mg in pregnancy). Prednisone percent unbound was lower in pregnancy (p=0.003). Only prednisolone total CL/F differed (see prednisolone).
source: Ryu RJ et al. J Clin Pharmacol 2018;58:1223-1232 PMID 29733485
notes: The library models total prednisone with a constant free fraction of 0.25 (Xu); pregnancy lowers the prednisone free fraction (higher CBG), but the measured total prednisone PK did not change, so no adjustment. Placental 11beta-HSD2 converts prednisolone to prednisone (fetal protection), not represented.

finding: Hodge 2026 (read in full; renal impairment was an exclusion, so normal renal function): population PK in 10 women at term caesarean (median 78 kg): sugammadex two-compartment, central V1 6.82 L, total V 13.9 L, CL 8.03 L/h, 'at the upper end of published ranges from non-pregnant patients'. No control arm. The library's Kleijn 2011 model, for a 30-year-old 78 kg woman with the library's assumed creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (Cockcroft-Gault 126.6 mL/min), gives CL = 5.58 x [1 + 0.00378 x 3.5] x [2 x 126.6/(126.6+119)]^1.29 = 5.88 L/h (Hodge/Kleijn = 1.36), Vc + Vp = 4.86 + 6.91 = 11.8 L (13.9/11.8 = 1.18). Sugammadex is cleared almost entirely unchanged by the kidney.
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the clearance term only, when the serum creatinine is left blank; the peripheral-volume term keeps the unadjusted value. Reproduces Hodge 2026's 8.0 L/h at term to within 8%.
comparator: published non-pregnant model (Kleijn 2011, the library's own)
design: popPK (uncontrolled) checked against the library model
source: Hodge AT, Tognolini AR, Liu X, et al. Plasma levels and postpartum breastmilk concentrations of sugammadex: a pharmacokinetic study in women undergoing general anaesthesia for caesarean delivery. Int J Obstet Anesth 2026;66:104874 PMID 41747364
notes: Total sugammadex (free + complexed) as in the library. Pregnant serum creatinine is physiologically lower (~0.5-0.6 mg/dL, memory); if the user enters a measured value, Cockcroft-Gault already reflects the GFR rise and the 1.5 factor should not be applied on top (the library should apply x1.5 only to the assumed-normal creatinine path, or accept double counting). Cockcroft-Gault with pregnant total weight also inflates CR. Kleijn's weight term uses total weight.

finding: No pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of neostigmine was found (searches for neostigmine with pregnancy/caesarean/postpartum and pharmacokinetics returned none).
notes: From memory only (not verified this session): roughly half of neostigmine clearance is renal and clearance falls markedly in renal failure (Cronnelly R et al., Anesthesiology 1979).
