To apply the general GFR rise, it would be cl1 x (1 - fe + 1.5 fe) ~ x1.25 for fe ~0.5, but this is unverified.

finding: Ali-Melkkila 1990 (read in full): 8 women given 6 ug/kg into the deltoid an hour before caesarean section (69.8 kg), radioreceptor assay: Cmax 6.3 ng/mL at 10 min, half-life 33.4 min, AUC(0-8 h) 5.61 ng.h/mL, systemic clearance (dose / AUC, absorption taken as complete) 1.12 (0.23) L/h/kg, 58% of the dose in the urine by 8 h. The same group with the same assay had measured 0.58 L/h/kg after the same intramuscular route and 0.54 L/h/kg intravenously in nonpregnant gynaecological patients; the authors attribute the faster clearance and shorter half-life to the cardiac output, plasma volume and renal clearance of pregnancy. The library model (Bartels 2013) gives 0.54 L/h/kg of cation for a nonpregnant woman of the parturients' size, the same nonpregnant reference.
applied: Clearance × 1.9 (1.12 / 0.58 L/h/kg, parturients over nonpregnant patients, both intramuscular, one laboratory and assay); volumes and distribution clearances unchanged.
comparator: nonpregnant gynaecological patients of the same laboratory (cross-study)
design: NCA against the same laboratory's nonpregnant studies
source: Ali-Melkkila T, Kaila T, Kanto J, Iisalo E. Pharmacokinetics of glycopyrronium in parturients. Anaesthesia 1990;45:634-637 PMID 2400072; Kirvela M, Ali-Melkkila T, Kaila T, Iisalo E, Lindgren L. Pharmacokinetics of glycopyrronium in uraemic patients. Br J Anaesth 1993;71:437-439 PMID 8398530; Kaila T, Ali-Melkkila T, Iisalo E, Kanto J. Radioreceptor assay for pharmacokinetic studies of glycopyrrolate. Pharmacol Toxicol 1990;67:313-316 PMID 2077523
to_obtain: Ali-Melkkila TM, Kaila T, Kanto J, Iisalo E. Pharmacokinetics of intramuscular glycopyrrolate. Br J Anaesth (1990): the nonpregnant intramuscular comparator (0.58 L/h/kg), to confirm its patients and dose basis.
notes: Radioreceptor assay (active cation plus any active metabolites). Library model is the active cation per bromide-labelled dose; the ratio is taken within one laboratory, so the dose basis cancels. The intramuscular dose is assumed wholly absorbed in both studies; the faster Tmax in pregnancy (10 vs 16 min) is not applied, the model being intravenous.

finding: No mannitol PK study in pregnancy found. Mannitol is eliminated by glomerular filtration without reabsorption; its clearance is used as a GFR surrogate (Deferm 2021).
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the renal term when the serum creatinine is left blank, so clearance × 1.5 (physiological: mannitol is a filtration marker); volumes unchanged.
source: Deferm N et al. Glomerular filtration rate in asphyxiated neonates under therapeutic whole-body hypothermia, quantified by mannitol clearance. Clin Pharmacokinet 2021;60:897-906 PMID 33611729
notes: The plotted quantity is serum osmolality; baseline osmolality in late pregnancy is ~10 mOsm/kg lower (physiology, not retrieved here), which the user sets via the osmolality covariate. Renal term is Cockcroft-Gault on the entered weight and creatinine. If the user enters the pregnant woman's ACTUAL serum creatinine (typically 0.4-0.6 mg/dL at term) and actual weight, CG already reports much of the GFR rise, and multiplying by 1.5 double-counts. The 1.5 factor is cleanest when the creatinine field is blank (assumed normal nonpregnant creatinine); the library applies one policy for all renal drugs (cefazolin/gentamicin/vancomycin already multiply unconditionally).

finding: The model (Ansari 2025) was fitted in 55 parturients at cesarean delivery (median 39 weeks, mean weight 80 kg, bleeding ~800 mL) given calcium chloride or gluconate after cord clamping; no nonpregnant data exist in the source. No other study of the ionized-calcium time course after IV calcium in pregnant vs nonpregnant adults was searched for beyond the model file.
source: Ansari JR, Conti DJ, Michel G, Yarmosh A, Cole NM, Shafer SL. Bioequivalence and pharmacokinetics of intravenous calcium during cesarean delivery. Anesthesiology 2025;142:121-131 PMID 39361822
notes: Plotted quantity is the CHANGE in ionized calcium above baseline. The model file (R/drugs_calcium.R) also records median gestation 39 weeks and mean weight 79.8 kg.

finding: No human pregnancy PK study found; only a five-case series measuring maternal/cord/milk concentrations (Plomp 1992) without PK parameters, and reviews. R/pregnancy.R notes Ansari 2016 names amiodarone only in its text.
source: Plomp TA, Vulsma T, de Vijlder JJ. Use of amiodarone during pregnancy. Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 1992;43:201-7 PMID 1563571
notes: Desethylamiodarone metabolite also unaffected. Amiodarone is avoided in pregnancy except for life-threatening arrhythmia.

finding: As for amiodarone: no pregnancy PK data for intravenous amiodarone found.
source: Plomp TA et al. Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 1992;43:201-7 PMID 1563571
notes: Highly protein bound (96%); unquantified free-fraction change.

finding: Westin 2017 (Norwegian paired TDM, same women pregnant vs own baseline) found dose-adjusted serum escitalopram +7% in mid-third trimester (NS, p=0.55), from 97 escitalopram pregnancies; the parent/metabolite ratio rose +40%, consistent with mild CYP2C19 downregulation. Schoretsanitis 2020 meta-analysis combined alteration ratio 1.10 (13 patients). Both conclude dose adjustment is not needed. escitalopram is pure S-enantiomer; CYP2C19-metabolized (the stanpumpR model carries a CYP2C19 phenotype).
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; Schoretsanitis G, Spigset O, Stingl JC, Deligiannidis KM, Paulzen M, Westin AA. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008
notes: Library plots total (here single-enantiomer) concentration; Westin measured total escitalopram. Model not fitted in pregnant women; flag currently does nothing (escitalopram does not name `pregnant`).

finding: Westin 2017 (58 citalopram pregnancies, paired TDM) found dose-adjusted total serum citalopram -24% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -38 to -7, p=0.007). Heikkinen 2002 (11 pregnancies) found -42%; Sit 2008 (small n). Schoretsanitis 2020 meta combined ratio 0.70. The decline is driven mainly by the inactive R-enantiomer (CYP2D6 induced in pregnancy); the active S-enantiomer (=escitalopram, CYP2C19) changes little.
applied: Clearance × 1.32 (total citalopram −24%, Westin 2017); volumes unchanged. Most of the fall is the inactive R-enantiomer.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; Heikkinen T, Ekblad U, Kero P, Ekblad S, Laine K. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2002;72(2):184-91 PMID 12189365; Schoretsanitis G et al. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008
notes: Library plots TOTAL R+S citalopram (what the AGNP band and Westin refer to). Because the fall is mostly the inactive R-enantiomer, the total 1.32x clearance overstates the change in therapeutic (S) exposure. Model (Akil 2016) fitted in Alzheimer patients, not pregnant women.

finding: Sertraline is the one antidepressant whose dose-adjusted serum concentration RISES in pregnancy. Westin 2017 (34 women/37 pregnancies, paired TDM) found +68% in mid-third trimester (95% CI +37 to +106, p<0.001); desmethylsertraline +120%. Schoretsanitis 2020 meta combined ratio 1.38 (18 patients). Heinonen 2021 found 3rd-trimester dose-adjusted concentration 0.19 vs 0.25 postpartum (67% relative difference, direction consistent). Freeman 2008 (longitudinal, n=6-9) found nonsignificant mean changes with large between-subject heterogeneity (lowest AUC/Cmax in third trimester for 5/6). Mechanism likely CYP2C19 inhibition. Monfort 2024 (ConcePTION perinatal popPK, 38 women, read in full) found NO significant gestational-age or pregnancy covariate on sertraline CL/F (only CYP2C19 phenotype, which did not survive in the final model), so it neither refines nor contradicts the Westin factor.
applied: Clearance × 0.60 (concentration +68%, Westin 2017): the one drug whose clearance falls; volumes and absorption unchanged.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; Schoretsanitis G et al. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008; Heinonen E et al. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2021;77(9):1323-1331 PMID 33751155; Freeman MP et al. J Clin Psychopharmacol 2008;28(6):646-53 PMID 19011433
notes: stanpumpR sertraline model (Alhadab 2020, ABSOLUTE parameters anchored by IV data, healthy adults) plots total plasma sertraline, which is what Westin measured. The sertraline header already cites Monfort 2024 as not mixed in. Pregnancy LOWERS clearance here (opposite direction to all the others).

finding: Paroxetine shows the largest decline. Westin 2017 (20 pregnancies, paired TDM) found dose-adjusted serum paroxetine -51% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -66 to -30, p<0.001); the authors recommend roughly a 100% dose increase to maintain levels. Ververs 2009 (74 pregnancies, longitudinal with CYP2D6 genotyping) found the effect is genotype-dependent: in extensive/ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers concentration fell 0.3 ug/L per gestational week (~30% by week 34), whereas in intermediate/poor metabolizers it ROSE 0.82 ug/L per week. Schoretsanitis 2020 meta ratio 0.82 (4 patients, statistical method differences).
applied: CL/F × 2.0 (concentration −51%, Westin 2017); V/F and absorption unchanged. Population-typical: in CYP2D6 poor and intermediate metabolisers paroxetine rises instead.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; Ververs FFT, Voorbij HAM, Zwarts P, Belitser SV, Egberts TCG, Visser GHA, Schobben AFAM. Clin Pharmacokinet 2009;48(10):677-83 PMID 19743889; Schoretsanitis G et al. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008
notes: Library plots total serum paroxetine. Model (Kim 2015) apparent one-compartment, fitted in Korean outpatients (assumed mostly CYP2D6 EM, like the Westin cohort). Direction reverses in CYP2D6 IM/PM - the single x2 factor is population-typical, not individualized.

finding: No dedicated duloxetine pregnancy popPK or paired longitudinal study with a usable ratio was retrieved. Leutritz 2022 (naturalistic TDM, 60 mothers) reported a DECREASE in serum duloxetine from first to second trimester but gives no quantitative ratio in the retrievable text. Boyce 2011 is a single-case placental/milk transfer report (cord/maternal 0.12), not a maternal PK-change study. Duloxetine is cleared by CYP1A2 (major) and CYP2D6; CYP1A2 activity falls while CYP2D6 rises in pregnancy, so net direction is uncertain.
source: Leutritz AL et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2023;89(2):737-750 PMID 36103361; Boyce PM, Hackett LP, Ilett KF. Arch Womens Ment Health 2011;14(2):169-72 PMID 21359876
to_obtain: Leutritz AL et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2023;89(2):737-750 (PMID 36103361): Full text may contain a quantitative trimester-by-trimester dose-adjusted concentration ratio for duloxetine that would let a cl1 factor be derived; the abstract gives direction only.
notes: Library plots total plasma duloxetine (apparent one-compartment, Zhong 2026). Model not fitted in pregnant women. CYP1A2 vs CYP2D6 opposing effects make the net direction uncertain.

finding: No human mirtazapine pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found (PubMed searches for 'mirtazapine pregnancy plasma/serum concentration pharmacokinetics' returned zero results). Mirtazapine is metabolized by CYP2D6, CYP3A4 and CYP1A2; these move in opposite directions in pregnancy, so even the net direction is unpredictable.
notes: No tool result returned any mirtazapine pregnancy PK paper. Model (Yan 2026) is apparent one-compartment in Chinese inpatients, not pregnant. Mixed CYP2D6/CYP3A4/CYP1A2 metabolism; direction unknown.

finding: Two paired pregnancy-vs-postpartum PK studies agree there is no clinically meaningful change. Fay 2021 (n=8, steady-state stereoselective) found no significant change in steady-state plasma concentrations, metabolite/parent ratios, formation clearances or renal clearance of bupropion or its metabolites during pregnancy vs postpartum. Fokina 2016 (n=28) likewise found no difference in oral clearance of bupropion or the OH-bupropion/bupropion metabolic ratio across pregnancy; a pregnancy-induced rise in CYP2B6 hydroxylation was offset by increased OH-bupropion glucuronidation and renal elimination, leaving exposure to the active OH-bupropion metabolite essentially unchanged.
source: Fay EE, Czuba LC, Sager JE, Shum S, Stephenson-Famy A, Isoherranen N. Ther Drug Monit 2021;43(6):780-788 PMID 33814540; Fokina VM et al. Drug Metab Dispos 2016;44(11):1832-1838 PMID 27528039
notes: Library plots bupropion + hydroxybupropion (both active). Model (Ghimire 2026) is apparent two-compartment for each. Pregnancy effects on parent and active metabolite are both negligible.

finding: Westin 2017 (43 pregnancies, paired TDM) found the active moiety (fluoxetine + norfluoxetine) -13% in mid-third trimester (NS); within that, fluoxetine fell -31% (NS, p=0.089) while norfluoxetine was unchanged (0%), and the parent/metabolite ratio fell -36% (p=0.01), reflecting CYP2D6-induced conversion of fluoxetine to norfluoxetine. Heikkinen 2003 (11 pregnancies) found active moiety -32% with the decline mainly in parent. Schoretsanitis 2020 meta active-moiety ratio 0.86. All conclude dose adjustment is generally not needed.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; Heikkinen T, Ekblad U, Palo P, Laine K. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2003;73(4):330-7 PMID 12709723; Schoretsanitis G et al. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008
notes: stanpumpR fluoxetine model (Han 2025) is valid only for the steady-state trough, with FM=1 parent->norfluoxetine formation. The parent declines ~31% but the plotted active moiety (both rows, no band) is essentially unchanged; a faithful pregnancy model would need separate parent and metabolite clearance increases, so the single-factor flag is left off.

finding: Westin 2017 (33 pregnancies, paired TDM) found the active moiety (venlafaxine + O-desmethylvenlafaxine, ODV) -22% in mid-third trimester (NS, p=0.16); parent venlafaxine declined (-40%, borderline) while ODV was unchanged (-13%, NS), with the ODV/venlafaxine ratio trending up (CYP2D6 induction). ter Horst 2014 (7 pregnancies) found venlafaxine ~87-100% of postpartum across trimesters (NS to -13%), ODV unchanged, and the ODV/venlafaxine ratio rising from 77% (T1) to 197% (T3). Schoretsanitis 2020 meta active-moiety ratio 1.00. A 2025 maternal-fetal PBPK (Choi 2025) predicts venlafaxine+ODV fall with gestation needing up to 225 mg in T3, but is model-based with n=7-9.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Spigset O. PLoS One 2017;12(7):e0181082 PMID 28708853; ter Horst PGJ et al. J Clin Pharm Ther 2014;39(5):541-4 PMID 24989434; Schoretsanitis G et al. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol 2020;16(5):431-440 PMID 32238008; Choi SY, Yang E, Shin KH. Drug Des Devel Ther 2025;19:10367-10382 PMID 41312050
notes: Library plots venlafaxine and desvenlafaxine (ODV) as a pair; parent cl1 is the V->ODV conversion. Active moiety is what matters and is ~unchanged. PBPK (Choi 2025) argues for T3 dose increases but is low-n and model-based; not applied.

finding: No human methylphenidate pregnancy pharmacokinetic study with maternal concentrations was found; searches returned only teratogenicity/safety reviews, meconium/biofluid assay methods and FASD-child genotype work. Methylphenidate (d-MPH) is hydrolyzed mainly by carboxylesterase-1 (CES1), not by CYP; the effect of pregnancy on CES1 activity is essentially uncharacterized, so even the direction is unknown.
source: Ornoy A. Pharm Res 2018;35(3):46 (ADHD drugs in pregnancy/lactation review) PMID 29411149
notes: stanpumpR 'methylphenidate' is the adult d-MPH transit/two-compartment model (Lyauk 2016). CES1-cleared, so the usual CYP pregnancy reasoning does not apply. No maternal pregnancy PK.

finding: This is a children's model (Shader 1999, ages 5-18, total methylphenidate) and plots a different analyte (d+l) from the adult entry. There is no methylphenidate pregnancy PK literature at all, and the pregnant flag is intended for adults (PREGNANCY_MIN_AGE 12 means a pregnant adolescent is theoretically in range, but no pediatric-pregnancy PK exists). CES1-cleared.
notes: Pediatric model; CES1-metabolized total methylphenidate. No maternal pregnancy PK. Do not apply a pregnancy factor.

finding: No human lisdexamfetamine pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found (searches returned stimulant-in-pregnancy epidemiology/safety and biofluid assays only). The stanpumpR model is a pediatric d-amphetamine model (Tsuda 2020). Lisdexamfetamine is hydrolyzed by red-cell peptidases to d-amphetamine; amphetamine is eliminated by CYP2D6 and pH-dependent renal excretion. Pregnancy effects on these (CYP2D6 induction up; urinary pH variable) are not quantified for amphetamine, and there are no maternal concentration data.
source: Ornoy A. Pharm Res 2018;35(3):46 PMID 29411149
notes: Pediatric d-amphetamine model (Tsuda 2020), prodrug hydrolysis subsumed in empirical first-order input. No maternal pregnancy PK; CYP2D6 + renal-pH elimination, direction unknown.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of mixed amphetamine salts (Adderall) was found. The stanpumpR model is a children's d-amphetamine curve fitted to published pediatric group means (McGough 2003 and labels). Amphetamine is eliminated by CYP2D6 and pH-dependent renal excretion; pregnancy effects are not quantified and no maternal concentration data exist.
source: Smid MC, Metz TD, Gordon AJ. Clin Obstet Gynecol 2019;62(1):168-184 (stimulant use in pregnancy review) PMID 30601144
notes: Pediatric Adderall d-amphetamine model, no published popPK even in nonpregnant adults. No maternal pregnancy PK; amphetamine CYP2D6 + renal-pH elimination, direction unknown.

finding: Elkomy 2015 fitted a two-compartment popPK model to 20 non-pregnant women (elective surgery) and 40 term pregnant women (elective caesarean) given 4 or 8 mg IV, testing pregnancy as a categorical covariate and gestational age as continuous: neither was significant (p>0.05); dose was (8 mg reduced CL by 31% and Vss by 26% relative to 4 mg). A single-patient case (Lemon 2016) on oral ondansetron found apparent oral clearance rising from 12.6 (14 weeks) to 20.7 L/h (35 weeks), i.e. x 1.64 versus early pregnancy, with no postpartum comparison.
source: Elkomy MH et al. Ondansetron pharmacokinetics in pregnant women and neonates: towards a new treatment for neonatal abstinence syndrome. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2015;97:167-76 PMID 25670522; Lemon LS et al. Ondansetron Exposure Changes in a Pregnant Woman. Pharmacotherapy 2016;36:e139-41 PMID 27374186
notes: The opposing CYP changes of pregnancy (CYP1A2 down, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 up) are the authors' explanation for no net change. Lemon's case is oral (first-pass) and single-subject, so it does not bear on the IV model. The existing Ansari row ('no change in steady-state concentrations in the first trimester') is consistent.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic data for aprepitant in pregnancy were found (searches returned only contraceptive-interaction notes, tocolysis repurposing in mice and oncology risk-factor papers).
notes: Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate (and moderate inhibitor/inducer), so pregnancy-induced CYP3A4 activity would be expected to raise its clearance; direction only, not quantified. Highly protein bound (>95%).

finding: No human pharmacokinetic data for fosaprepitant or for aprepitant after fosaprepitant in pregnancy were found.
notes: As aprepitant. The prodrug conversion (phosphatases) is not expected to be rate-limiting in pregnancy.

finding: Quetiapine shows the largest antipsychotic decline. Westin 2017 (35 pregnancies, paired TDM, same women) found dose-adjusted serum quetiapine -76% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -83 to -66, p<0.001); the authors state doubling the daily dose may be needed in T3. A prior case report found trough -42/-55/-53% across trimesters. Zheng 2020 PBPK predicts AUC -49.1% in T3 and recommends at least a 2.5x dose. Quetiapine is CYP3A4-metabolized (induced in pregnancy).
applied: CL/F × 4.2 (concentration −76%, Westin 2017, paired); V/F and absorption unchanged. A PBPK model predicts about half this change.
source: Westin AA, Brekke M, Molden E, Skogvoll E, Castberg I, Spigset O. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331; Zheng L, Tang S, Tang R, Xu M, Jiang X, Wang L. Clin Pharmacokinet 2020;60(5):623-635 PMID 33251573
notes: Library plots total plasma quetiapine (apparent one-compartment, Zheng 2024, immediate release). D2 occupancy (Nord 2011) tracks plasma; MEAC and band are zero. Model not fitted in pregnant women. The TDM (-76%) and PBPK (AUC -49%) disagree substantially; the chosen 4.2x is the direct-measurement value.

finding: Westin 2017 (4 pregnancies only) found the risperidone active moiety (risperidone + 9-hydroxyrisperidone/paliperidone) -25% in mid-third trimester (NS, wide CI -63 to +54); the parent/metabolite ratio fell -37%. Mahdy 2023 PBPK (validated against Westin's cohort and an individual patient) quantifies the mechanism: at 40 weeks risperidone total clearance x1.61 and paliperidone total clearance x1.95 vs non-pregnant, driven by ~3x CYP2D6 induction (intrinsic CYP2D6 clearance x3.15); parent oral bioavailability also falls (F 0.52->0.26). Risperidone is CYP2D6/CYP3A4-metabolized to paliperidone. Not applied: the measured change is −25% and not significant in 4 women; the larger factors (× 1.6 parent, × 1.95 metabolite) are a PBPK prediction.
source: Westin AA et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331; Mahdy WYB, Yamamoto K, Ito T, et al. Clin Transl Sci 2023;16(4):618-630 PMID 36655374; Yano I. Nihon Yakurigaku Zasshi 2025;160(2):103-107 PMID 40024695
notes: Library plots risperidone + 9-hydroxyrisperidone (hydroxyrisperidone), serum, metabolite scaled by F.fmet with kFormation = cl1/v1. The two factors (parent 1.6, metabolite 1.95) come from PBPK; direct TDM is NS/n=4. CYP2D6 induction is the mechanism and the model already has a CYP2D6 phenotype.

finding: Westin 2017 (14 pregnancies, paired TDM) found the aripiprazole active moiety (aripiprazole + dehydroaripiprazole) -52% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -62 to -39, p<0.001); parent alone fell similarly, and the parent/metabolite ratio fell -31% (p<0.001). An earlier case series found concentrations fell >two-thirds and returned to baseline 2-3 weeks postpartum. Zheng 2020 PBPK predicts the active moiety AUC -60.9% in T3 and recommends ~2x dose. Aripiprazole is metabolized by CYP2D6 to dehydroaripiprazole, then CYP3A4; CYP2D6 is induced in pregnancy.
applied: Parent CL/F × 2.1 (Westin 2017: active moiety −52%); volumes, absorption and dehydroaripiprazole's own clearance unchanged, so the parent falls 52% and the plotted active moiety about 38%.
source: Westin AA et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331; Zheng L, Tang S, Tang R, Xu M, Jiang X, Wang L. Clin Pharmacokinet 2020;60(5):623-635 PMID 33251573
notes: Library plots aripiprazole + dehydroaripiprazole (plasma), metabolite scaled by fm, kFormation = cl1/v1. Model (Kim 2008, abstract-verified) carries a CYP2D6 phenotype. TDM (-52%) and PBPK (-61%) agree reasonably; chosen 2.1x from direct TDM.

finding: Westin 2017 (29 pregnancies, paired TDM) found dose-adjusted serum olanzapine -9% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -28 to +14, p=0.40), i.e. no significant change. Zheng 2022 PBPK predicts only a minor (<28%) decrease across pregnancy and concludes dose adjustment can hardly be recommended. Olanzapine is metabolized largely by CYP1A2 (activity falls in pregnancy) and UGT1A4 (induced), which offset each other; reduced smoking in pregnancy further lowers CYP1A2.
source: Westin AA et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331; Zheng L, Yang H, Dallmann A, Jiang X, Wang L, Hu W. Front Pharmacol 2022;12:793346 PMID 35126130
notes: Library plots total plasma olanzapine (apparent two-compartment, Sun 2021). CYP1A2/UGT1A4 opposing effects net to no change. Model not fitted in pregnant women.

finding: Westin 2017 (only 2 pregnancies) found dose-adjusted serum haloperidol -52% in mid-third trimester (95% CI -74 to -10). The 2026 systematic review (Adhayanti) repeats this '-52% in the third trimester' figure. Evidence is very limited (n=2) and no p-value was given. Haloperidol is metabolized by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, both of which can be induced in pregnancy. Not applied: the −52% is from 2 pregnancies.
source: Westin AA et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331; Adhayanti I, Robiyanto R, Bahar MA, Wahyudin E. Arch Womens Ment Health 2026;29(1):16 PMID 41528499
notes: stanpumpR 'haloperidol' is the ORAL apparent model (Pilla Reddy 2013, unverified brief values). Library plots total plasma haloperidol. The -52% rests on only 2 pregnancies; a conservative reading would prefer 'direction only'.

finding: No intravenous-haloperidol pregnancy PK study exists. The only human haloperidol pregnancy data are the oral TDM of Westin 2017 (-52% dose-adjusted serum concentration in T3, n=2), reflecting increased hepatic clearance (CYP2D6/CYP3A4). Because the IV model (Li 2022, critically ill adults) shares the same hepatic elimination enzymes, the same clearance increase is expected to apply to the absolute IV clearance. Not applied: no intravenous data; the oral −52% is from 2 pregnancies.
source: Westin AA et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2017;103(3):477-484 PMID 28643331
notes: ABSOLUTE IV model (Li 2022), not oral x F. No IV pregnancy data; the x2.1 is extrapolated from oral TDM via the shared CYP2D6/CYP3A4 elimination. Plasma total concentration. Could legitimately be classified 'unknown/direction only'.

finding: No intravenous droperidol maternal pharmacokinetic study in pregnancy was found. Retrieved droperidol+pregnancy papers are clinical (e.g. epidural droperidol to reduce morphine pruritus at cesarean) or ED headache use, not maternal PK. Droperidol is a butyrophenone cleared by hepatic CYP3A4 (and others); CYP3A4 is induced in pregnancy, suggesting clearance may rise, but no quantitative human pregnancy datum exists.
source: Horta ML, Ramos L, Goncalves ZR. Anesth Analg 2000;90(3):638-41 (epidural droperidol, cesarean; PD not PK) PMID 10702450
notes: stanpumpR 'droperidol' is the IV three-compartment model (Lehmann 1988), plasma, plasma-only. No maternal PK in pregnancy. CYP3A4 induction direction only.

finding: No intramuscular droperidol pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. As with IV droperidol, only clinical/PD reports in obstetric settings were found. Droperidol is hepatically metabolized (CYP3A4); pregnancy may increase clearance, but there is no quantitative human pregnancy datum, and IM absorption changes in pregnancy are not characterized for this drug.
notes: stanpumpR 'droperidolIM' is the apparent IM model (Foo 2016, acutely agitated patients), plasma-only. No maternal PK in pregnancy.

finding: Gin & Chan 1994 (read in full; Anesthesiology 81:829-832): human isoflurane MAC by a transcutaneous tetanic stimulus (not skin incision) was 0.775% (0.675-0.825) in 10 women at 8-12 weeks against 1.075% (1.025-1.175) in 10 nonpregnant women, a 28% fall (P < 0.001), with progesterone 63.4 vs 8.4 nM. Palahniuk 1974 (read in full; Anesthesiology 41:82-83): in 6 pregnant ewes within 3 weeks of term against 6 nonpregnant ewes of the same flock (tail-clamp stimulus), MAC was 25% lower for halothane (0.73 vs 0.97%), 40% for isoflurane (1.01 vs 1.58%) and 32% for methoxyflurane (0.18 vs 0.26%), all P < 0.025; the authors suggest progesterone. No measurement of nitrous oxide MAC or uptake in pregnancy was found. The volatile-agent data (27-30% reduction) may not transfer to nitrous oxide, whose mechanism (NMDA antagonism) differs. Animal data: rats -16% at term (Strout 1981), no change in mice/rats for halothane, isoflurane, enflurane (Mazze 1985); ewes (Palahniuk 1974, title only).
trimester: first (8-13 weeks) and immediate postpartum; no term human MAC study
comparator: non-pregnant women; women >72 h or >6 weeks postpartum
source: Gin T, Chan MT. Decreased minimum alveolar concentration of isoflurane in pregnant humans. Anesthesiology 1994;81:829-832 PMID 7943833; Chan MT, Mainland P, Gin T. Minimum alveolar concentration of halothane and enflurane are decreased in early pregnancy. Anesthesiology 1996;85:782-786 PMID 8873548; Chan MT, Gin T. Postpartum changes in the minimum alveolar concentration of isoflurane. Anesthesiology 1995;82:1360-1363 PMID 7793649; Zhou HH, Norman P, DeLima LG, Mehta M, Bass D. The minimum alveolar concentration of isoflurane in patients undergoing bilateral tubal ligation in the postpartum period. Anesthesiology 1995;82:1364-1368 PMID 7793650; Ueyama H, Hagihira S, Takashina M, Nakae A, Mashimo T. Pregnancy does not enhance volatile anesthetic sensitivity on the brain: an electroencephalographic analysis study. Anesthesiology 2010;113:577-584 PMID 20693882; Lee J, Lee J, Ko S. The relationship between serum progesterone concentration and anesthetic and analgesic requirements: a prospective observational study of parturients undergoing cesarean delivery. Anesth Analg 2014;119:901-905 PMID 25036373; Palahniuk RJ, Shnider SM, Eger EI 2nd. Pregnancy decreases the requirement for inhaled anesthetic agents. Anesthesiology 1974;41:82-83 PMID 4857789; Strout CD, Nahrwold ML. Halothane requirement during pregnancy and lactation in rats. Anesthesiology 1981;55:322-323 PMID 7270956; Mazze RI, Rice SA, Baden JM. Halothane, isoflurane, and enflurane MAC in pregnant and nonpregnant female and male mice and rats. Anesthesiology 1985;62:339-341 PMID 3977116
notes: Uptake (PK) side: no human study of volatile uptake or washout in pregnancy was retrieved. finding: Prospective population-based study (Tomson 1994, 93 pregnancies, 70 on carbamazepine or phenytoin monotherapy, dose kept constant unless seizures forced an increase, baseline >=10 weeks postpartum): TOTAL phenytoin in the third trimester was 39% of baseline, UNBOUND phenytoin 82% of baseline. The companion paper says total plasma clearance rose from the first trimester while unbound clearance rose less and only significantly in the third trimester. Lander 1977 (n=10) found the same direction. Yerby 1990 (read in full; 14 women on phenytoin, baseline 8 weeks postpartum): free fraction 10.1% against 7.7% in the third trimester (1.31) and 13% at delivery (1.69); total clearance 40 against 23 (1.74), free clearance 392 against 281 (1.40), Table VII; 57% of the women had their dose raised. The unbound clearance agrees with the model (x1.27 at constant dose); the measured free fraction is smaller than the 2.1-fold rise derived from Tomson's ratio of means. Dam 1979 (read in full) is an independent check: with doses adjusted to hold the level, the ratio of dose over trough level at weeks 37-40 to that after delivery in 7 women was 1.08, 1.14, 3.33, 2.02, 1.61, 1.37, 1.22 (median 1.37), and the two factors predict 1.37 at 15 mg/L.
applied: Km (total) × 0.48, from the doubled unbound fraction, and Vmax × 1.1, so a typical 15 mg/L total falls to 39% (Tomson 1994) while the unbound concentration falls only to 82%.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of diamorphine (heroin) was found. finding: Catalano 1998 (read in full; hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp in 16 women): metabolic clearance rate of insulin 422 mL/m2/min before conception, 514 at 12-14 weeks, 526 at 34-36 weeks, so 526/422 = 1.25 late over pregravid (P = 0.0005). Per m2 of body surface area; Tham CL/F carries no size covariate, so the absolute ratio is nearer 1.35 (x1.08 for the ~8% rise in surface area), and 1.25 is applied as a measured lower bound. Insulin requirements in late pregnancy rise mostly through insulin resistance (pharmacodynamics, not plotted). Clearance: Catalano 1998 measured the metabolic clearance rate (MCR) of infused insulin by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp in 16 women before conception, at 12-14 and at 34-36 weeks: MCR 442 -> 514 -> 526 mL/m^2/min (late/pregravid 1.19, per m^2 BSA, p = 0.0005), no difference between normal and abnormal glucose tolerance. Goudie 2015 (Bayesian popPK of insulin aspart by CSII, 22 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, 12-33 weeks): MCR per kg fell a non-notable 0.33%/week of gestation, while time-to-peak rose 1.7% per week (a ~30 min gestational delay in time-to-peak from early to late pregnancy had been reported earlier).
applied: CL/F × 1.25 (Catalano 1998, 526/422 mL/m2/min, late over pregravid), on every product through thamInsulin(); absorption and V/F unchanged. Per m2: the absolute ratio is nearer 1.35 and 1.25 is a conservative lower bound.
trimester: third (34-36 weeks) for MCR; 12-33 weeks for aspart absorption
comparator: same women before conception (Catalano); within-pregnancy gestational trend (Goudie)

to_obtain: Goudie 2014 (insulin aspart) was read in full: it is a letter with no usable model (the equations are in Haidar 2013, not supplied) and it concerns insulin aspart, which is NOT one of the library's Tham 2017 insulins, so it cannot firm up these models. No applicable pregnancy source for the Tham insulins was found.
notes: All Tham 2017 insulins come from thamInsulin() in R/insulinTham.R, so one pregnancy branch there covers every product. Tham's V/F scales with (BW/80)^1.62 (human insulins) or ^2.48 (lispro) or linearly (glargine): entering a term-pregnant weight inflates V/F by weight alone (e.g. 70 -> 82 kg gives x1.29 for human insulin, x1.48 for lispro), an effect not supported by any pregnancy data; the library may want the pregnancy branch to evaluate the weight terms at pre-pregnancy weight or to note it. Catalano's MCR is a systemic clearance of IV insulin at clamp concentrations, applied here to the apparent CL/F on the assumption that SC bioavailability is unchanged (no data). Insulin is not protein bound; total = free (immunoassay of exogenous + endogenous insulin in Catalano, corrected for residual secretion by C-peptide).

finding: Liao 2020 (read in full; OPRU network, steady-state NCA, GDM at 26-38 weeks): pregnant women with GDM on metformin 500 mg (n = 24 monotherapy, 30 with glyburide) against nonpregnant women with T2DM (n = 24). At 500 mg CL/F was 27% higher and V/F 33% higher in pregnancy; bioavailability, CL, renal CL and Vbeta all rose (F rose enough at 1000 mg to cancel the CL/F change at that dose). Eyal 2010 (OPRU, longitudinal, read in full; n = 35 pregnant / 16 postpartum, paired): metformin renal clearance 625 +/- 130 mL/min late pregnancy vs 477 +/- 132 postpartum (ratio 1.31; mid pregnancy 723 -> 1.52), creatinine clearance 419 vs 313 mL/min (1.34) and net secretion 207 vs 165 (1.25); but apparent oral CL/F was only 1759 vs 1590 mL/min late (+11%, N.S.) and 2038 mid (+28%, N.S.), with V/F and half-life unchanged, so the renal rise is largely offset in the apparent oral clearance the library uses. Charles 2006 popPK (third trimester, cross-study only) reported CL/F 28 L/h/70 kg and concluded no difference from nonpregnant patients, a discordant cross-study comparison.
applied: CL/F × 1.27 and V/F × 1.33 (Liao 2020 at 500 mg); the creatinine clearance term is not also raised, which would count the filtration rise twice.

If the user enters a pregnant woman's (lower) serum creatinine, Cockcroft-Gault will already raise CLcr; the library documents that the pregnancy factor is meant for the assumed-normal creatinine. Eyal 2010's paired apparent oral CL/F rose only 11% (late, N.S.), so Liao's 1.27 (cross-sectional at 500 mg) sits at the upper end of the evidence.

finding: Hebert 2009 (OPRU, steady state): 40 women with GDM at 28-38 weeks vs 26 nonpregnant women with T2DM. Compartmental CL/F 18.3 +/- 10.3 vs 9.6 +/- 6.9 L/h (ratio 1.91); NCA CL/F 17.6 vs 9.0 L/h in CYP2C9*1/*1 (1.96) and 13.7 vs 6.9 in variant carriers (1.99). V/F 83 +/- 65 vs 53 +/- 36 L (1.57). finding: The library model is intravenous unfractionated heparin plotted as anti-IIa activity (Jia 2015, cardiopulmonary bypass, absolute CL=1.18 L/h, no covariates). Human pregnancy PK exists only for SUBCUTANEOUS prophylaxis: Brancazio 1995 gave 143 U/kg SC to 6 third-trimester women vs 6 non-pregnant controls and found peak plasma heparin 0.11 vs 0.23 U/mL (half as high) with shorter time-to-peak; Whitfield 1983 showed a reduced heparin anticoagulant slope (1.68 vs 2.33 ml/U) in third-trimester women, i.e. relative heparin resistance from increased heparin-binding proteins, factor VIII and fibrinogen (confirmed in vitro by Chunilal 2002). These describe lower free-heparin activity per dose and a higher dose requirement, not an intravenous clearance factor.

notes: Renal elimination (~20%) could rise ~1.5x with the pregnancy GFR increase, but renal is a minor pathway and no drug-specific data exist; do not apply speculatively.

finding: Enoxaparin has the best pregnancy PK data of any drug in the library. Lebaudy 2008 (popPK, 75 pregnant vs 38 non-pregnant women) found apparent clearance higher throughout pregnancy, 0.78 L/h vs 0.52 L/h (0.78/0.52 = 1.50), stage-independent, with the volume of distribution rising in two steps including an additional +41% in the last 2 months independent of weight. Patel 2013 (popPK, 123 antenatal women, 795 anti-Xa values) found both clearance and volume increased during pregnancy and the half-life prolonged. Casele 1999 (paired, 13 women early/late pregnancy vs 6-8 wk postpartum, 40 mg SC) found AUC and Cmax significantly lower in pregnancy than in the same women postpartum. The Zarek 2025 systematic review summarises a ~1.5-fold increase in apparent CL with ~30% AUC reduction and 30-50% V expansion.

comparator: non-pregnant women (Lebaudy) and same women postpartum (Casele)

EULAR Rheumatol Open 2025;1:11-22 PMID 42367607
notes: The library plots anti-Xa activity (total). Renal excretion is only ~15-20% of enoxaparin CL, so the 1.5x total-CL rise is NOT simply a GFR effect (Zarek: a sole renal mechanism would need a 3-10x renal increase); it reflects increased non-renal (reticuloendothelial) clearance too, so apply the factor directly to cl1 rather than via the CrCl term. The model's CrCl term (exponent 0.25) stays as is. verified: abstract for the numbers; the Zarek review was read in full text.

finding: No population PK model with a pregnancy covariate was found. Fondaparinux is eliminated almost entirely by renal excretion of unchanged drug (unlike LMWH), so the pregnancy GFR rise (~50%) is the expected mechanism of any clearance increase; the Wu 2025 state-of-the-art review notes it crosses the placenta and that renal insufficiency raises accumulation/bleeding risk, implying renal clearance dominates. No pregnant-vs-control PK ratio is reported. By analogy to the heparins the Zarek review grouped (all ~1.5x apparent CL in pregnancy), exposure is expected to fall, requiring anti-Xa monitoring.
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the renal term of CL/F when the serum creatinine is left blank, so CL/F × 1.24 (physiological: no fondaparinux data).
source: Wu Y, Ji Y, Wang S, Hu Y, Shan D. Arch Gynecol Obstet 2025;312:1461-1471 PMID 40938418; Zarek J, Brydon A, Spitzer K, Laskin C, Ito S. EULAR Rheumatol Open 2025;1:11-22 PMID 42367607
to_obtain: Delavenne X, et al. (POP-A-RIX). Thromb Haemost 2010;104:252-260 and any obstetric fondaparinux PK series: No fondaparinux pregnancy PK ratio was found; a dedicated pregnant-vs-nonpregnant anti-Xa PK study (if one exists) would be needed to replace the GFR-analogy estimate.
notes: Plotted curve is plasma fondaparinux (mg/L), apparent parameters. Because elimination is almost entirely renal, the GFR term is the right place to apply a pregnancy change; the library's standard 1.5x GFR rise is defensible here where it is not for the enoxaparin model.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant contraindicated in pregnancy; it crosses the placenta (ex vivo and PBPK reports) and the literature is confined to inadvertent-exposure registries and placental-transfer work, none giving a pregnant-vs-nonpregnant CL/F ratio. The model is from non-pregnant NVAF/ACS/healthy subjects (Cirincione 2018).
notes: Renal elimination ~27% plus CYP3A4/P-gp; CYP3A4 induction and GFR rise in pregnancy would predict increased CL/F (lower exposure), but there is no quantification and the drug is contraindicated, so no adjustment.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. Rivaroxaban is a DOAC contraindicated in pregnancy. The only pregnancy/peripartum signals are a case of possible postpartum treatment failure attributed to pregnancy-related PK changes reducing exposure (Rudd 2015) and a breast-milk case report (Wiesen 2016); neither gives maternal antepartum PK. The model is pooled non-pregnant patients (Willmann 2018).
source: Rudd KM, Winans ARM, Panneerselvam N. Pharmacotherapy 2015;35:e164-8 PMID 26598101; Wiesen MHJ, Blaich C, Muller C, et al. Chest 2016;150:e1-4 PMID 27396794
notes: The postpartum failure report is anecdotal and directional only; it cannot support a factor. CYP3A4 induction + renal rise would predict higher CL/F but is unquantified.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. Edoxaban is a DOAC contraindicated in pregnancy; no pregnant-vs-nonpregnant PK data were found. The model is pooled phase 1 and Hokusai-VTE non-pregnant patients (Niebecker 2015).
notes: Edoxaban is ~50% renally cleared; a GFR rise would raise CL/F, but no data and contraindicated, so no adjustment.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study exists. Dabigatran (and its prodrug etexilate) is a DOAC contraindicated in pregnancy. The only direct pregnancy data is an ex vivo dually-perfused placenta study (Bapat 2014) showing transplacental transfer (fetal-to-maternal ratio 0.33 for dabigatran), which measures placental transfer, not maternal disposition. The model is non-pregnant RE-LY atrial fibrillation patients (Liesenfeld 2011).
source: Bapat P, Kedar R, Lubetsky A, et al. Obstet Gynecol 2014;123:1256-1261 PMID 24807346
notes: Dabigatran is ~80% renally cleared; the pregnancy GFR rise would raise CL/F, but there is no maternal PK study and the drug is contraindicated, so no adjustment. The Bapat data concern fetal exposure only.

finding: No clean human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of S-/R-warfarin clearance was found. Warfarin is a teratogen generally avoided in pregnancy (used only for some mechanical heart valves). Reported pregnancy warfarin dose requirements change, but this is dominated by pharmacodynamic shifts in clotting-factor and vitamin-K-dependent protein turnover (the very turnover the model embeds), not by a measured change in enantiomer clearance, so a PK factor cannot be separated out.
to_obtain: Any S-/R-warfarin enantiomer pharmacokinetic study in pregnant women (CYP2C9 substrate; CYP2C9 activity is reported to rise in pregnancy): To separate a true clearance change from the PD clotting-factor changes; none was retrievable in this session.
notes: Plotted output is INR, not concentration. S-warfarin is a CYP2C9 substrate and CYP2C9 activity is thought to increase in pregnancy (would raise S-warfarin CL), but no quantified pregnancy enantiomer PK was found and the drug is contraindicated except for mechanical valves.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found. Fluindione is an indane-dione vitamin-K antagonist, a known teratogen contraindicated in pregnancy (notably associated with fetopathy); it is used in France outside pregnancy. The model is 24 healthy non-pregnant volunteers (Verstuyft 2012).
notes: Plotted output is INR via an indirect-response model; no pregnancy PK or PD data.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found. Acenocoumarol is a coumarin vitamin-K antagonist, a teratogen contraindicated in pregnancy (used in Europe outside pregnancy, occasionally for mechanical valves). The model is 24 healthy non-pregnant volunteers, S-enantiomer (Verstuyft 2012).
notes: Plotted output is INR via an indirect-response model; no pregnancy PK or PD data. S-acenocoumarol is a CYP2C9 substrate.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found. The only direct evidence is animal: Morishima 1992 infused IV cocaine in pregnant vs non-pregnant rats and found LOWER maternal plasma cocaine in pregnancy with enhanced cardiovascular response and limited placental transfer (fetal/maternal 0.28). Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (which hydrolyses cocaine) falls in pregnancy, which could in principle slow hydrolysis and raise concentration, but the rat data point the other way and no human quantification exists. Direction is therefore uncertain.
source: Morishima HO, Cooper TB, Hara T, Miller ED. Dev Pharmacol Ther 1992;19:69-79 PMID 1340439
notes: Model is intranasal parent cocaine in plasma (opt-in research model). The butyrylcholinesterase decline of pregnancy is the plausible human mechanism but is unquantified for cocaine and opposed by the rat finding; no adjustment.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study was found. Pregnancy methamphetamine literature concerns neurodevelopmental outcomes and placental/fetal transfer in animals, not maternal disposition. The model is the d-enantiomer given intranasally to non-pregnant experienced users (Harris/Cook).
notes: Methamphetamine is partly CYP2D6-metabolised and partly renally excreted (pH-dependent); pregnancy could alter both but no human quantification. No adjustment.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of LSD was found. The model is apparent oral parameters in non-pregnant healthy adults (Dolder). No maternal disposition data in pregnancy exist.
notes: Apparent oral parameters; no pregnancy data.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of psilocybin/psilocin was found. The model is apparent oral parameters (free psilocin plotted) in non-pregnant healthy adults (Holze). No maternal disposition data in pregnancy exist.
notes: Psilocin is glucuronidated (UGT) and partly renally handled; UGT activity rises in pregnancy but no psilocin data. No adjustment.

finding: No human maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of MDMA was found. The retrievable pregnancy literature is animal/synthetic-cathinone placental-transfer work (e.g. Strange 2017, bath salts in mice), not human MDMA disposition. The model is apparent oral parameters in non-pregnant healthy adults (Huestis).
source: Strange LG, Kochelek K, Keasling R, Brown SD, Pond BB. Neurotoxicol Teratol 2017;63:9-13 PMID 28811141
notes: MDMA is CYP2D6/CYP3A4-metabolised with autoinhibition (nonlinear); pregnancy enzyme changes are unquantified for MDMA. The cited study is a mouse cathinone model, used only to confirm no human MDMA pregnancy PK exists. No adjustment.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic data in pregnancy. PubMed has 8 records naming clevidipine with pregnancy or preeclampsia: case reports (e.g. Brazeal 2025, severe preeclampsia) and reviews, none with concentrations. Clevidipine is hydrolysed by blood and tissue esterases, so a large pregnancy change in clearance is not expected, but none has been measured.
source: Brazeal C, Shapiro A. Use of intravenous clevidipine in the management of severe preeclampsia: a case report. Cureus 2025;17:e99287 PMID 41542001
notes: The model plots whole-blood concentration from healthy volunteers (Ericsson 1999). Plasma cholinesterase falls in pregnancy, but clevidipine is hydrolysed by red-cell and tissue esterases (statement from memory, not verified here), so the fall in plasma cholinesterase is no reason to change it.

finding: A children's model (Hammer 2008: children under general anaesthesia). There are no human pregnancy pharmacokinetic data for fenoldopam (no PubMed record combining fenoldopam, pregnancy and pharmacokinetics).
notes: The app shows the Pregnant control only for women of PREGNANCY_MIN_AGE and older, but a pregnant adolescent given this pediatric model should still get no adjustment, because there is no evidence to base one on.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study found. A combined PubMed search (carvedilol, hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone or procainamide, with pregnan* and pharmacokinetic* in title or abstract) returned no carvedilol study. Carvedilol is a high-extraction drug with extensive first-pass metabolism by CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and UGTs. Two other drugs like it rise in apparent oral clearance in late pregnancy: metoprolol (CYP2D6, CL/F x3.0) and labetalol (glucuronidation, CL/F x1.6). So carvedilol's CL/F probably rises too, but by an unmeasured amount.
source: Fischer JH, Sarto GE, Hardman J, et al. Influence of gestational age and body weight on the pharmacokinetics of labetalol in pregnancy. Clin Pharmacokinet 2014;53 (pages not retrieved) PMID 24297680
notes: The model is apparent oral (/F) with zero-order release, from 21 healthy Korean men (Hwang 2023). Its parameters are all /F, so any pregnancy change in first-pass extraction would appear as a change in every /F parameter.

finding: Angiotensin-receptor blockers are contraindicated in the second and third trimesters for fetal toxicity, so there are no pregnancy pharmacokinetic studies. A review on losartan, retrieved here, states the class contraindication.
source: Sica DA, Gehr TW, Ghosh S. Clinical pharmacokinetics of losartan. Clin Pharmacokinet 2005;44:797-814 PMID 16029066
notes: The quote is about losartan and the ARB class, not azilsartan specifically.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. A combined search (with hydrochlorothiazide, carvedilol, procainamide) returned no chlorthalidone pregnancy study. Thiazide-type diuretics are used little in pregnancy.
notes: The model's large apparent volumes reflect partitioning into red cells (about 95% of the drug in whole blood). The haematocrit falls in pregnancy (haemodilution), which could raise the plasma fraction, but this is unquantified and not recommended.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. (combined search with chlorthalidone, carvedilol and procainamide: none for HCTZ). Hydrochlorothiazide is eliminated almost entirely unchanged in urine, by filtration and tubular secretion. The model's clearance is Cockcroft-Gault-driven renal clearance plus a small nonrenal clearance (Van Wart 2013).
applied: Renal clearance × 1.5 when the serum creatinine is left blank (physiological: no hydrochlorothiazide data); nonrenal clearance and volumes unchanged.
source: Ansari J, Carvalho B, Shafer SL, Flood P. Anesth Analg 2016;122:786-804 (the rise in glomerular filtration of pregnancy)
notes: The renal term is clR = 18.3 L/h x (crcl/120)^1.38 (HCTZ_CL_R_EXP = 1.38). So 1.5x crcl gives clR x 1.5^1.38 = 1.75, and at the reference crcl total clearance x (18.3 x 1.75 + 2.44)/(18.3 + 2.44) = 1.66 (arithmetic done here). For the GFR rise to mean a 1.5x renal clearance, multiply clR (not crcl) by 1.5, giving total x1.46. I lean to clR x1.5, since the 1.38 exponent describes renal disease, not hyperfiltration. As with the antibiotics, a measured pregnant creatinine already carries part of the GFR rise, so a 1.5x on top double-counts it. That caveat is shared with the existing GFR-adjusted models. Fraction excreted unchanged: from memory (>95%), not verified.

finding: No human study of exogenous epinephrine pharmacokinetics in pregnancy was found (a PubMed search on catecholamine clearance in pregnant women returned nothing). The model is from adult septic shock (Abboud 2009), with SAPS II and an endogenous baseline.
notes: Catecholamines are cleared by neuronal and extraneuronal uptake and by COMT/MAO, with clearance near cardiac output. Cardiac output rises 30-50% in pregnancy (physiology from memory), which could raise clearance, but this is unmeasured. Do not apply.

finding: The model's own source, Du 2019 (PMC6518930, full text read), was fitted in 92 women with preeclampsia (mean gestational age 34.7 weeks, range 21-40.3). 43% of its 623 samples were drawn before delivery and 56% after it, during the 24 h postpartum infusion and 12 h of washout. Gestational age and age were not significant covariates on CL. Antepartum versus postpartum status entered only as an occasion for interoccasion variability, not as a fixed effect. Brookfield 2016 (the parent dataset, 111 women, read in full) found CL 3.98 L/h in preeclamptic and 5.88 L/h in non-preeclamptic pregnant women: one compartment, V 22.5 L x (WT/70), no weight term on CL, baseline Mg 1.96 mg/dL; the preeclamptic CL agrees with Du 2019 within 7%, and the non-preeclamptic population is one the library (Du 2019, preeclamptic) does not cover.
source: Du L, Wenning LA, Carvalho B, et al. Population pharmacokinetic modeling to evaluate standard magnesium sulfate treatments and alternative dosing regimens for women with preeclampsia. J Clin Pharmacol 2019;59:374-385 PMID 30422321; Brookfield KF, Su F, Elkomy MH, et al. Pharmacokinetics and placental transfer of magnesium sulfate in pregnant women. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2016;214:737.e1-9 PMID 26767791
notes: The library has no preeclampsia flag. Non-preeclamptic pregnant clearance is 5.88/3.98 = 1.48x the preeclamptic value. Most of that difference may already come through the model's creatinine term: a normal pregnant creatinine of 0.5 mg/dL gives (0.5/0.8)^-0.731 = 1.41x the clearance at the model's 0.8 reference (arithmetic done here). So entering the woman's measured creatinine is the right way to individualise. The concern is a blank creatinine field: the library then assumes 0.8 mg/dL for a woman (SCR_ASSUMED_FEMALE), which equals the model reference and is the median of these preeclamptic women, not of normotensive pregnancy. The model plots the change above baseline Mg, not total Mg.

finding: Rubin 1983 (read in full; 50 mg IV, 10 women in the last trimester of hypertensive pregnancy, 7 of them again postpartum, and 10 nonpregnant controls): clearance 2.16 vs 2.35 (postpartum) vs 1.96 (controls) L/min, Vss and half-life also no different between groups; pregnancy did not alter the disposition of intravenous labetalol. For INTRAVENOUS labetalol (this model's route), Rubin 1983 compared 10 hypertensive women in the third trimester, 7 of the same women postpartum and 10 non-pregnant controls. Clearance was 2.16 L/min pregnant vs 2.35 postpartum (ratio 0.92) and 1.96 in controls (ratio 1.10); volume of distribution was not different. ORAL labetalol differs: Fischer 2014 (popPK, 57 women, 649 samples, longitudinal) found CL/F 1.4x postpartum at 12 weeks and 1.6x at 40 weeks, and V/F 1.9x. The authors attribute this to higher hepatic intrinsic clearance (UGT1A1 induction) and more first-pass extraction, which an IV route is insensitive to for a high-extraction drug. Protein binding was unchanged (62%, 59%, 61% bound in T2, T3 and postpartum).
source: Rubin PC, Butters L, Kelman AW, Fitzsimons C, Reid JL. Labetalol disposition and concentration-effect relationships during pregnancy. Br J Clin Pharmacol 1983;15:465-470 PMID 6849783; Fischer JH, Sarto GE, Hardman J, et al. Influence of gestational age and body weight on the pharmacokinetics of labetalol in pregnancy. Clin Pharmacokinet 2014;53 (pages not retrieved) PMID 24297680; van de Vusse D, Mian P, Schoenmakers S, et al. Pharmacokinetics of the most commonly used antihypertensive drugs throughout pregnancy methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine: a systematic review. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2022;78 (issue and pages not retrieved) PMID 36104450; Rogers RC, Sibai BM, Whybrew WD. Labetalol pharmacokinetics in pregnancy-induced hypertension. Am J Obstet Gynecol 1990;162:362-366 PMID 2309815
notes: Fischer's discussion explicitly says IV administration (Rubin) is 'insensitive to pregnancy-related alterations in protein binding or hepatic enzyme activity compared to the oral route'. Rogers 1990 (oral, n=8, no comparator) reported a terminal half-life of 1.7 h vs 6-8 h in the literature and CL/F 21.8 mL/min/kg. Labetalol is plotted as total racemate. Labetalol is a first-line drug in pregnancy, so the help page should explain why the IV model is left unchanged.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. (combined verapamil/diltiazem search: transporter and placental studies only).
notes: Diltiazem is a CYP3A4 substrate. CYP3A activity rises in pregnancy (midazolam CL/F unbound 593 vs 345 L/min, x1.72, Hebert 2008), so oral diltiazem clearance would probably rise. This model is IV (Hoglund 1988, CL 992 mL/min), and for an intermediate-to-high extraction drug IV clearance would rise less. Unquantified; do not apply.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. Nitroglycerin is used as a uterine relaxant at delivery, but no pharmacokinetic study in parturients was found.
notes: Extremely high, largely extrahepatic (vascular, red-cell) clearance (6.2 L/min in the model's source). No basis for a pregnancy factor.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic study of norepinephrine in pregnancy was found. Norepinephrine is now used as a prophylactic infusion for spinal hypotension at cesarean delivery, but the PubMed searches returned dosing and haemodynamic studies, not concentrations.
notes: The model is from healthy volunteers awake (Li 2024) and plots exogenous NE above an endogenous baseline. The same physiological caveat as epinephrine applies (clearance tied to cardiac output, which rises in pregnancy), but it is unquantified.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. (combined search with HCTZ, chlorthalidone, carvedilol: none). In the model (Grasela 1984, standard individual), clearance is renal 14.4 L/h x renal fraction + acetylation 10.1 L/h + other 1.2 L/h. So about 56% is renal at normal renal function (14.4/25.7 = 0.56, from the model file).
applied: Renal clearance × 1.5 when the serum creatinine is left blank (physiological: no procainamide data); acetylation, other clearance and volume unchanged.
source: Ansari J, Carvalho B, Shafer SL, Flood P. Anesth Analg 2016;122:786-804 (the rise in glomerular filtration of pregnancy)
notes: Procainamide's renal clearance includes active tubular secretion (OCT2). Pregnancy raises secretion of other drugs too (digoxin secretion x1.88, Hebert 2008), so 1.5x on the renal fraction is not unreasonable, but it is an extrapolation. The NAT2 acetylation change in pregnancy is unknown. NAPA is not plotted. The usual double-counting caveat applies if a measured pregnant creatinine is entered.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. PubMed has only case reports (e.g. Gilson 1992, intrapartum esmolol with neonatal beta blockade).
source: Gilson GJ, Knieriem KJ, Smith JF, et al. Short-acting beta-adrenergic blockade and the fetus. A case report. J Reprod Med 1992;37:277-279 PMID 1348787
notes: Esmolol is hydrolysed by red-cell cytosolic esterase (from memory), not plasma cholinesterase, so the fall in pseudocholinesterase in pregnancy is not relevant. The model is whole blood (de Bruijn 1987).

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found.
notes: The model is from healthy men (MacGregor 2000). No basis for a factor.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. Only placental-transfer and review literature exist (e.g. Kanto & Klotz 1988, which notes atropine crosses the placenta readily). The model's source (Hinderling 1985 Table I, from R/drugs_atropine.R) gives CL 1175 mL/min, of which 656 mL/min (56%) is renal. That renal clearance exceeds GFR, so it is largely tubular secretion.
source: Kanto J, Klotz U. Pharmacokinetic implications for the clinical use of atropine, scopolamine and glycopyrrolate. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1988;32:69-78 PMID 3279717
notes: The renal fraction (656/1175 mL/min) is from the model file's own source, not from a PubMed retrieval in this session.

finding: Rubin 1987 gave intravenous propranolol 10 mg to 12 women with pregnancy-induced hypertension in the third trimester and again 2-3 months postpartum (paired), measuring whole blood. Clearance was 0.63 vs 0.71 L/h/kg (ratio 0.89) and Vss 4.02 vs 3.07 L/kg (ratio 1.31). The authors conclude that pregnancy did not alter disposition. The heart-rate response per ng/mL was greater in pregnancy (pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic).
source: Rubin PC, Butters L, McCabe R, Kelman A. The influence of pregnancy on drug action: concentration-effect modelling with propranolol. Clin Sci (Lond) 1987;73:47-52 PMID 3608376
to_obtain: O'Hare MF, et al. (propranolol pharmacokinetics in pregnancy, oral; cited elsewhere). Citation not retrieved in this session.: An oral study would show whether first-pass (CL/F) changes as for metoprolol. That does not affect this IV model, but would matter for an oral propranolol. The paper could not be located by PubMed search here.
notes: Rubin measured whole-blood propranolol; Fagan 1982 (the model) is plasma. The ratio, not the matrix, is what transfers. The model is IV-only.

finding: Hebert 2008 gave oral digoxin 0.25 mg to 13 women at 28-32 weeks and again at 6-10 weeks postpartum (paired). Unbound renal clearance was 272 vs 183 mL/min (x1.49) and unbound net secretion 109 vs 58 mL/min (x1.88), consistent with higher GFR and renal P-gp activity; the full text (now read) gives total renal clearance 163 vs 125 mL/min (x1.30), AUC0-48h 19% lower, and the terminal half-life unchanged (38.4 vs 46.5 h). Luxford & Kellaway 1983 (read in full; 15 women on 0.375 mg/day, third trimester against 6-16 weeks postpartum, paired): creatinine clearance 135.7 vs 97.8 mL/min/1.73m2 (x1.39), digoxin renal clearance 103.5 vs 85.7 (x1.21), 24-h urinary digoxin 185.6 vs 133.6 ug (x1.39), the renal-clearance rise matching the filtration rise, so no change in tubular handling; serum digoxin was higher in the third trimester (1.28 vs 1.01 ng/mL), which the authors attribute to greater absorption (slower gut transit) outrunning the faster elimination. Earlier text said digoxin renal clearance, creatinine clearance and 24-h urinary digoxin all fell significantly postpartum, but so did serum digoxin.
applied: Creatinine clearance × 1.5 in the renal term when the serum creatinine is left blank, reproducing Hebert's × 1.49 in renal clearance; the nonrenal term and volumes unchanged.
source: Hebert MF, Easterling TR, Kirby B, et al. Effects of pregnancy on CYP3A and P-glycoprotein activities as measured by disposition of midazolam and digoxin: a University of Washington specialized center of research study. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2008;84:248-253 PMID 18288078; Luxford AM, Kellaway GS. Pharmacokinetics of digoxin in pregnancy. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1983;25:117-121 PMID 6617713; Iisalo E. Clinical pharmacokinetics of digoxin. Clin Pharmacokinet 1977;2:1-16 PMID 322907
notes: Hebert's ratios are for UNBOUND clearance, but digoxin is only 20-30% bound (Iisalo), so total clearance changes almost the same. Caveat: digoxin-like immunoreactive substances rise in pregnancy and cross-react in immunoassays (from memory, not verified here). Luxford's higher third-trimester serum levels are explained in that paper by greater absorption; the library plots the apparent oral model, not serum from a fixed dose. The usual double-counting caveat applies if a measured (lower) pregnant creatinine is entered. Yukawa's parameters are /F; oral bioavailability in pregnancy is not known.

finding: Same evidence as digoxin: renal digoxin clearance is x1.49 in the third trimester vs postpartum (Hebert 2008, n=13, paired). About 72-75% of digoxin is cleared renally in healthy adults (Iisalo: 25-28% nonrenal). So total clearance rises by about 0.73 x 1.49 + 0.27 = 1.36 (arithmetic done here); Hebert's full text (now read) gives total renal clearance 163 vs 125 mL/min (x1.30), corroborating this.
applied: Clearance × 1.35 (renal clearance × 1.49 on about 73% of the clearance); volumes unchanged.
source: Hebert MF, Easterling TR, Kirby B, et al. Effects of pregnancy on CYP3A and P-glycoprotein activities as measured by disposition of midazolam and digoxin: a University of Washington specialized center of research study. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2008;84:248-253 PMID 18288078; Iisalo E. Clinical pharmacokinetics of digoxin. Clin Pharmacokinet 1977;2:1-16 PMID 322907
notes: Alternative if the library prefers the library's GFR convention: apply 1.5 to CLcr in the clearance regression only (not Vss), accepting the smaller (~1.15x) effect. I recommend the direct cl1 x1.35. Same immunoassay (DLIS) caveat as digoxin. The 87-min time to peak effect (Hornestam) is unchanged.

finding: A children's model (el-Desoky 2005, 0.33-15 years with heart failure). The pregnancy data (Hebert 2008) are for adult women.
notes: A pregnant adolescent would be better served by digoxinIV with its pregnancy adjustment than by this pediatric model.

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found. (combined verapamil/diltiazem search: only placental and transporter studies, e.g. verapamil as a P-gp probe in pregnant macaques).
notes: Verapamil is a high-extraction CYP3A4 substrate. CYP3A activity rises about 1.7x in pregnancy (midazolam CL/F unbound x1.72, Hebert 2008), which would raise oral CL/F substantially. IV clearance (this model, Kates 1981) is largely flow-limited and would change little. Unquantified; do not apply.

finding: No human pharmacokinetic study of phenylephrine in pregnancy was found, although it is the standard vasopressor for spinal hypotension at cesarean delivery. Ngan Kee 2009 measured maternal arterial and umbilical concentrations at delivery in 104 women randomised to phenylephrine or ephedrine infusions. It reported placental transfer (median umbilical venous/maternal arterial ratio 0.17 for phenylephrine vs 1.13 for ephedrine), not clearance; the full text (now read) gives maternal arterial phenylephrine 8.2 ng/mL at delivery and a median titrated dose of 100 ug, but with no defined steady-state infusion rate a clearance cannot be derived.
source: Ngan Kee WD, Khaw KS, Tan PE, Ng FF, Karmakar MK. Placental transfer and fetal metabolic effects of phenylephrine and ephedrine during spinal anesthesia for cesarean delivery. Anesthesiology 2009;111:506-512 PMID 19672175
notes: The model is serum free phenylephrine in 4 volunteers (Hengstmann 1982).

finding: Searched PubMed for human pregnancy pharmacokinetics; none found.
notes: Milrinone is excreted mainly unchanged in urine (about 80%, from memory, not verified here), so a GFR rise in pregnancy would raise clearance. Without a renal term or data, none is recommended. If the library wanted a physiological extrapolation: cl1 x (0.8 x 1.5 + 0.2) = 1.4, using an unverified renal fraction.

finding: A pediatric model (Hornik 2019, birth to 18 years). No pregnancy data.

Hogstedt 1985 (read in full; 5 women with hypertension, IV 10 mg and oral 100 mg in the third trimester and again 3-6 months postpartum): oral bioavailability 0.21 +/- 0.06 vs 0.42 +/- 0.05 (P < 0.01), systemic clearance 1.38 vs 0.65 L/min (postpartum 55% +/- 13% of pregnant, not significant), volume 6.87 vs 3.85 L/kg (not significant), half-lives identical (IV 5.38 vs 5.36 h, oral 3.42 vs 3.42 h), binding 9% vs 11%. Ryu 2015 (PMC5564514, full text) studied steady-state oral metoprolol across pregnancy, paired with the same women at 3 months or more postpartum. CL/F was 568 vs 192 L/h in late pregnancy (34-38 weeks, n=8; x2.96) and 361 vs 200 L/h in mid-pregnancy (n=5; x1.8). The metabolic ratio fell, consistent with CYP2D6 induction. The one CYP2D6 poor metaboliser had very low CL/F in pregnancy (0.37-0.41 L/h/kg). Hogstedt 1985 gave IV and oral doses to 5 women in late pregnancy and again 3-6 months postpartum. Oral bioavailability was 1.3-3.7x higher after pregnancy. Postpartum systemic (IV) clearance was 26-97% of the pregnant value, a difference that was not significant. Hogstedt 1983 (n=5) found CL/F 4.4x higher in late pregnancy. Protein binding was low and unchanged (9% vs 11%, per Ryu's discussion).
applied: Clearance, both volumes and Q × 1.5 and oral bioavailability × 0.5, so CL/F × 3.0 (Ryu 2015's 2.96) with every half-life unchanged (Hogstedt 1985: identical half-lives, bioavailability 0.21 vs 0.42); not applied to a CYP2D6 poor metaboliser.
source: Ryu RJ, Eyal S, Easterling TR, et al. Pharmacokinetics of metoprolol during pregnancy and lactation. J Clin Pharmacol 2016;56 (epub 2015; pages not retrieved) PMID 26461463; Hogstedt S, Lindberg B, Peng DR, Regardh CG, Rane A. Pregnancy-induced increase in metoprolol metabolism. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1985;37:688-692 PMID 4006368; Hogstedt S, Lindberg B, Rane A. Increased oral clearance of metoprolol in pregnancy. Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1983;24:217-220 PMID 6840170
notes: Ryu's 2.96 ratio is unadjusted for dose nonlinearity. In the subset on the same dose in both periods, CL/F was 551 vs 194 L/h (x2.84), consistent. Ryu reports a 2.6-fold weight-adjusted CL/F ratio in late pregnancy; because the model scales clearance with weight, one could use 2.6 on a per-kg basis (cl1 x1.45, F x0.55, by the same split). The difference is within the uncertainty. Total concentrations; fu is unchanged.

finding: Bartels 2007 (read in full; 10 pre-eclamptic women on continuous IV nicardipine 1-9 mg/h): maternal plasma 1.4-15.7 ng/mL, a placental-transfer and breast-milk study whose maternal samples are sparse, often not at steady state and confounded by pre-eclampsia, so no apparent clearance can be derived; umbilical/maternal ratio 0.15-0.17. No pharmacokinetic parameters for nicardipine in pregnancy were found. In preeclamptic women given IV nicardipine, Bartels 2006 (n=10) and Matsumura 2014 (n=18) report placental transfer (umbilical/maternal 0.15-0.17) and breast-milk transfer. Matsumura 2014 (read in full) computed an apparent clearance (dose over steady-state concentration) of 678 mL/h/kg at delivery vs 756 postpartum (n=17/16; medians 579 vs 626), with no difference delivery-vs-postpartum and both overlapping the healthy-adult range -- a crude dose/Css estimate in preeclamptic women, so no factor, but no sign of an important change in nicardipine clearance. Carbonne 1993 (oral and IV in 60 women) reports blood pressure only.
source: Bartels PA, Hanff LM, Mathot RA, et al. Nicardipine in pre-eclamptic patients: placental transfer and disposition in breast milk. BJOG 2007;114:230-233 PMID 17166219; Matsumura H, Takagi K, Seki H, et al. Placental transfer of intravenous nicardipine and disposition into breast milk during the control of hypertension in women with pre-eclampsia. Hypertens Pregnancy 2014;33:93-101 PMID 24131296; Carbonne B, Jannet D, Touboul C, Khelifati Y, Milliez J. Nicardipine treatment of hypertension during pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol 1993;81:908-914 PMID 8497354
notes: By analogy with nifedipine (oral CL/F about 2x in the third trimester, van de Vusse 2022 review) and CYP3A induction (Hebert 2008, midazolam x1.72), oral nicardipine would clear faster. This model is IV, and nicardipine has high hepatic extraction. A well-stirred estimate with E about 0.7 and a 1.7-2x rise in intrinsic clearance would raise IV clearance only 1.1-1.2x (arithmetic done here, assumption-laden). Not recommended without data.

finding: No human pregnancy pharmacokinetic study of GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate/sodium oxybate) was found. The model is two-compartment with saturable (Michaelis-Menten) elimination fitted to the non-pregnant narcolepsy (sodium oxybate) programme. No maternal disposition data in pregnancy exist.
notes: GHB is eliminated by saturable metabolism (GHB dehydrogenase, then the Krebs cycle), largely non-renal; a GFR shortcut does not apply and no pregnancy data exist.
